Sub: Notice of the 61st Annual General Meeting (“AGM”), Integrated Annual Report and Annual Accounts 
and other Reporting Suite for the Financial Year 2025-26 
 
Dear Sir/Madam, 
 
We wish to inform you that the 61st AGM of the Company is scheduled to be held on Tuesday, July 14, 2026 
at 3:00 p.m. IST through Video Conferencing (“VC”)/Other Audio-Visual Means (“OAVM”) in accordance 
with the circulars/notifications issued by the Ministry of Corporate Affairs (“MCA”) and the Securities and 
Exchange Board of India (“SEBI”) to transact the businesses as set forth in the Notice dated May 29, 2026 
convening the AGM (“Notice”). 
 
The other details for the AGM are given below:

Pursuant to Regulation 34(1) and 53(2) of the SEBI (Listing Obligations and Disclosure Requirements) 
Regulations, 2015 (“Listing Regulations”), as amended from time to time, please find enclosed herewith 
the Integrated Annual Report including the Annual Accounts and the Business Responsibility and 
Sustainability Report (“BRSR”) for the Financial Year 2025-26 (“Annual Report”) along with the AGM Notice 
being sent to all Members in electronic mode. 
 
With a vision focused on the future, Vedanta is transforming into a global natural resources, energy and 
technology leader. As India accelerates towards a new era of growth, Vedanta 2.0 is building the 
foundations of tomorrow through critical minerals, energy, technology and world-class resources. By 
expanding capacity, embracing innovation and advancing sustainability, we are powering growth, enabling 
progress and creating enduring value for all stakeholders. Driven by operational excellence and a 
commitment to nation-building, we are shaping a stronger, more resilient and sustainable future for 
generations to come. 
 
In this regard, the Company has also published the following reports (“Reporting Suite”) for FY 2025–26 
for gaining insight into the Company’s performance:  
1. Tax Transparency Report 
2. Sustainability Report 
3. Climate Action Report 

 
 
 
The aforementioned reports and the AGM Notice have been made available on the website of the Company 
as below:  
Sr. No. 
Name of the Report

www.vedantalimited.com

Pursuant to Section 91 of the Companies Act, 2013 read with Rule 10 of the Companies (Management and 
Administration) Rules, 2014, the Register of Members and Share Transfer Books of the Company will 
remain closed from Thursday, 09 July 2026 to Monday, 13 July 2026 (both days inclusive) for the purpose 
of AGM. 
 
We request you to please take the above on record. 
  
Thanking you, 
 
Yours faithfully, 
For Vedanta Limited

Vedanta Limited, a 
subsidiary of Vedanta 
Resources Limited, is a 
global natural resources 
conglomerate. Our strategic 
asset base across India, 
Africa and the Middle 
East positions us to serve 
growing global demand. We 
operate across zinc-lead-
silver, iron ore, steel, copper, 
aluminium, power, nickel, 
and oil and gas, holding 
market-leading positions in 
several of these businesses. 
Integrated reporting
Integrated Reporting explains 
how we create, preserve and, 
where relevant, erode value 
over time, aligned with our 
purpose, strategy and values. 
Since adopting Integrated 
Reporting in FY 2017-18, we have 
strengthened integrated thinking 
and continuously enhanced 
our disclosures.
The FY 2025-26 report presents 
a comprehensive view of our 
material matters, their impact 
on the environment and society, 
and the associated risks and 
opportunities influencing business 
performance. It supports an 
informed assessment of our 
ability to create value across the 
short, medium and long term.
Scope and boundary
The Integrated Report and Annual 
Accounts 2025-26 cover the reporting 
period from 01 April 2025 to 31 March 
2026 and provides a comprehensive 
overview of Vedanta Limited (Vedanta, 
VEDL), a subsidiary of Vedanta 
Resources Limited.
It reflects performance across our 
business segments: zinc-lead-silver, 
oil and gas, aluminium, power, iron 
ore, steel, nickel and copper. Our 
assets span India, South Africa and 
the Middle East, covering the full value 
chain from exploration and asset 
development to extraction, processing 
and value-addition.
The report explains our performance, 
strategy and value creation model 
through an interlinked multi-
capital framework. It also outlines 
stakeholder engagement practices, 
governance structures and risk 
management processes.
Approach to stakeholder 
engagement and materiality
Our stakeholders include individuals 
and organisations whose interests or 
actions influence our ability to execute 
strategy and sustain performance. We 
engage regularly with key stakeholder 
groups to understand expectations and 
address concerns.
This report focusses on material matters 
that affect our capacity to create value 
over the short, medium and long term.
Annual accounts
This report should be read alongside 
the Annual Accounts (pages 428 to 
725) for a complete understanding of 
VEDL’s financial performance.
The consolidated and standalone 
financial statements have been 
prepared in accordance with Indian 
Accounting Standards (Ind AS) 
notified under the Companies (Indian 
Accounting Standards) Rules, 2015, 
as amended. These statements 
have been independently audited 
by S.R. Batliboi & Co. LLP. The 
Independent Auditors’ Reports for 
consolidated and standalone financial 
statements appear on pages 428 and 
725 respectively.
Board and management assurance

Company’s management accept 
responsibility for the integrity and 
completeness of information 
presented in this report. To the 
best of their knowledge, the report 
addresses all material matters and 
fairly represents the integrated 
performance, position and impacts of 
Vedanta Limited.

statements’ – that is, statements 
about business expectations and

our expected future business and

competitive or regulatory nature.

actual future results to be materially

THE TRANSITION

performance and operational excellence with ESG priorities, stakeholder interests and emerging market 
opportunities. It informs our strategic choices, including our transition to Vedanta 2.0. Through this strategic 
transformation, we are repositioning our portfolio aligned with India’s needs in energy transition, critical minerals, 
advanced manufacturing, and clean technologies, while harnessing AI, automation, and innovation to drive agility 
and future-readiness. Our ‘Transforming for Good’ ESG framework remains a guiding force. Embedded across 
operations, it supports responsible growth, disciplined risk management and strengthens business resilience.

Defining what matters for lasting impact
Sustained business performance and responsible operations are two sides of the same commitment. In 
FY 2025-26, we conducted our Double Materiality Assessment through an independently facilitated process, 
engaging approximately 1,600 internal and external stakeholders across surveys, interviews, focussed group 
discussions, and 14 site visits. The assessment examined 26 material topics through two lenses:
Financial materiality: Considering how sustainability issues affect our business performance and capital.
Impact materiality: Considering how our operations affect people, ecosystems, and economies.
The results directly shape how we allocate resources, set targets, and strengthen disclosures across our 
Transforming for Good framework. A clearer understanding of which topics carry the highest financial and 
impact significance enables us to manage emerging risks proactively, respond to evolving stakeholder 
expectations, and pursue opportunities that create lasting value for our business and the communities we serve.

Purpose of Double Materiality 
Assessment (DMA)
We conduct a detailed materiality 
assessment every two years, with an 
annual management review, to identify 
and prioritise the topics that matter 
most to our stakeholders and our 
business. Our previous assessment 
was conducted in FY 2022-23, guided 
by GRI Standards 2021. Building on that 
foundation, our FY 2025-26 exercise was 
independently facilitated and aligned 
with the principles of the EU Corporate 
Sustainability Reporting Directive (CSRD) 
and leading sector standards, including 
GRI, ICMM, and SASB, and evaluated 
positive and negative impacts, risks, and 
opportunities associated with each of our 
26 material topics. The findings inform 
how we set targets, allocate resources, 
and strengthen disclosures across the 
Vedanta Group. Additionally, the key KPIs 
for our material topics are aligned with 
annual independent assurance and audit 
requirements, ensuring we consistently 
meet our own standards and relevant 
industry benchmarks. The findings enable 
us to align our reporting with evolving 
stakeholder expectations, integrate 
material ESG risks into our enterprise 
risk management processes, and 
reinforce our commitment to long-term 
value creation and responsible business 
performance across the Vedanta Group.
Materiality determination 
process
Our approach to materiality determination 
examines each topic through the lens 
of strategy, risk, capital, and global 
sustainability priorities to ensure that 
what we disclose and manage genuinely 
what matters most. By integrating 
these elements, we aim to deliver 
long-term value for our stakeholders 
while contributing to broader societal 
and environmental goals and ensuring 
alignment with the UN Sustainable 
Development Goals. For each of our 
26 material topics, we ensured that our 
sustainability commitments remain

Identify potential material topics by analysing company disclosures 
and benchmarking against peer reports, global standards (including

Engage key internal and external stakeholders through surveys, 
interviews, and focussed discussions to validate and prioritise IROs. 
Over 1,625 internal and external stakeholders were consulted, and 
inputs were scored to assess impact significance (scope, scale, 
likelihood, irremediability) and financial risks and opportunities 
(magnitude and likelihood).

Stakeholder engagement
Review and validate the materiality outcomes with senior leadership, 
followed by final approval from the Board-level ESG Committee. The 
overall process and results were also subjected to independent third-
party assurance to ensure transparency and credibility.

Validation and review
Identify and map positive and negative impacts, and financial risks 
and opportunities for each material topic using internal sources (risk 
registers, human rights and community assessments) and external 
inputs (peer reports, media, GRI, SASB, and rating methodologies). 
This resulted in 250+ IROs, with key risks further assessed for 
potential financial impact.
2
Map Impacts, Risks, and Opportunities (IRO)
Score material topics based on stakeholder inputs and apply 
weightings for stakeholder influence and interest, along with 
revenue-based weightages to derive group-level prioritisation, 
resulting in a consolidated materiality matrix across financial and 
impact dimensions.

methodology, independently facilitated and informed by leading 
international frameworks. We analysed both dimensions of 
materiality, systematically examining how sustainability issues

With a steadfast commitment to sustainability, ethical governance, and community stewardship, Vedanta 
integrates ESG principles into the architecture of its operations, aligning with global benchmarks and 
contributing to India’s progress toward self-reliance, inclusive prosperity, and long-term resilience.

our ESG commitments translate into measurable outcomes.

Our three-pronged social strategy, “Do

our presence at source. Building Trust 
is maintained through continuous, 
transparent dialogue and grievance 
mechanisms that communities 
can use, are accessible in local 
languages, and are resolved with 
accountability. Benefit Sharing ensures 
that the economic value generated 
by our operations flows back into 
host communities through local 
employment, local procurement, and 
development programmes designed 
around what communities need rather 
than what is convenient to deliver.

seek informed consent before any 
project that may affect indigenous 
lands or resources, and approach 
land acquisition and resettlement 
with legal compliance and 
community consultation as non-
negotiable conditions.

TRANSFORMING THE PLANET
Embedding environmental responsibility into our business model
The scale of what we do and the environmental footprint it carries are not things we describe in the abstract. 
It is the operational reality from which our environmental commitments are built, and it is the reason those 
commitments must be specific, time-bound, and backed by capital rather than language. The metals we produce 
are essential to the global clean energy transition: aluminium for electric vehicles and solar panels, zinc for 
galvanised infrastructure, copper for transmission networks, and silver for solar technologies. This creates a 
fundamental tension; industries that supply materials for a greener economy must also decarbonise, conserve 
water, and manage waste responsibly. We address this challenge directly through clearly defined targets, 
committed capital, and the operational programmes.
Decarbonisation
We are committed to net zero carbon emissions

low-carbon driven. As the country's 
premier metals and mining company,

ambitious national goals of reaching

by 2030 and achieving net zero 
emissions by 2070. By aligning our 
near-term actions with these national 
objectives, we are contributing 
meaningfully to India's broader 
climate goals and the transition to a 
sustainable future.
Our Net Zero ambition reflects a clear

four‑phase roadmap spanning

Renewable energy is our

signed 1.03 GW of round-the-clock

tangible results at scale. At TSPL,

Securing water for the future
Water is one of the most critical resources shaping the future of both industry and communities. Notably, 81.8% of our 
business units operate in high water-stress regions, particularly in Rajasthan, where our zinc, lead, and silver businesses 
draw from catchments under sustained climatic and demand pressure. Responsible management is fundamental to 
our operational resilience and long-term sustainability. We recognise water as a shared resource, and our approach 
reflects this principle.
For communities in Bhilwara, Jharsuguda, and the Barmer basin, water underpins livelihoods, food security, and daily 
life. Our operations draw from the same catchments, making it essential that our presence strengthens, rather than 
strains, local water systems. These realities make our target of achieving net water positivity (greater than 1) by 2030 
not aspirational, but essential.

The metals and mining sector carries 
a unique environmental obligation, not 
just to reduce what it extracts from 
the earth, but also to manage the 
resulting impacts with discipline and 
accountability. Every tonne of metal 
we produce generates by-products 
that must be handled responsibly, 
emissions that must be monitored and 
minimised, tailings that must be stored 
safely, and land whose biodiversity 
must be protected and restored. Aim 
6 addresses all these dimensions 
through continuous improvement, 
innovation, and governance that holds 
us accountable at every level.
Advanced monitoring systems 
ensure the safety and integrity of 
tailings facilities, while biodiversity 
is safeguarded through a “Do No 
Harm” approach aligned with global 
standards to minimise environmental 
impact. This is reinforced by our 
Resource Use and Waste Management 
Technical Standard, which prioritises 
reduction and avoidance at source, 
followed by recovery and recycling, 
with disposal treated strictly as a last 
resort. Together, these measures 
support our long-term ambition 
of achieving 100% utilisation of 
hazardous and high-volume, low-
toxicity waste by 2035.
These efforts are managed as part 
of an integrated system rather 
than isolated initiatives. Advancing 
circularity in waste streams improves 
resource efficiency and supports 
cost optimisation. Robust tailings 
management safeguards operational 
continuity and mitigates risk. 
Investments in biodiversity protection 
and restoration contribute to stronger 
community relationships and long-
term site viability. Together, these 
actions reflect a cohesive approach 
to environmental management, 
where operational performance 
and responsible practices are 
closely aligned.
Waste to wealth: Turning by-
products into resources
Vedanta has established a Group-
wide Waste to Wealth programme 
that converts industrial by-products 
into commercially viable resources, 
advancing circularity across all 
operations. The programme is built 
on the principle that waste generated 
at one point in the value chain is a 
resource for another, and Vedanta's 
scale creates the opportunity to

Our operations carry inherent risks

and every serious incident reflects a 
failure of the system that allowed it 
to occur. This conviction drives our 
safety architecture, from the Board 
ESG Committee to the individual site 
safety officer.
Our framework is anchored in 
Critical Risk Management, which 
systematically addresses key 
operational risks through defined 
protocols and accountability 
mechanisms. When incidents occur, 
the Incident Cause Analysis Method 
(ICAM) drives structured investigation: 
identifying root causes rather than 
surface-level explanations and 
implementing targeted corrective 
actions to prevent recurrence. The 
Safety Community of Practice 
oversees implementation across all 
sites, with performance independently 
audited through VSAP and aligned 
with ISO 45001, OHSAS 18001, and 
International Council on Mining and

adherence to global best practices.

We have identified three critical focus areas to strengthen safety performance and prevent serious incidents across our operations.

safety

Group-wide priority for identifying and

digital tools, automation, and AI-driven 
systems across business units to

safety oversight.

Our commitment to workforce 
well-being extends across both 
physical and mental health. Mantra

employee wellness programme,

Structured incident 
investigation: the ICAM 
approach
Learning from incidents is as 
important as preventing them. 
Vedanta adopts the Incident Cause 
Analysis Method (ICAM) as its 
standard framework for investigating 
health and safety incidents across 
all operations. ICAM is a structured 
methodology that goes beyond 
surface-level explanations to 
systematically identify the underlying 
and root causes of an incident 
examining individual actions, team and 
supervisory factors, work environment 
conditions, and organisational 
systems that contributed to the event.
Where a conventional investigation 
might conclude with an immediate 
cause, ICAM goes deeper: uncovering 
the latent organisational conditions 
that enabled the incident and 
prescribing corrective actions at every 
level of the causal chain. This enables 
Vedanta to refine safety protocols 
with precision, close systemic gaps 
before they produce further incidents, 
and embed learning permanently 
into operational practice rather than 
treating it as a post-incident formality.
Through ICAM, Vedanta reinforces its 
commitment to maintaining safety 
standards that meet and consistently 
exceed international benchmarks 
reflecting the organisation's broader 
conviction that a safer operation is 
not only a more responsible one, but a 
more productive and sustainable one 
for all stakeholders.

Impact on Vedanta
The deployment of Vedanta Group's 
first all-women locomotive engine 
team at the Jharsuguda aluminium 
smelter, marking a significant 
milestone in its inclusion agenda. By 
placing women at the helm of one 
of the plant's most critical logistical 
operations, Vedanta Aluminium has 
demonstrated that the commitment 
to gender equity extends to every 
function, including those that have 
historically been the most resistant 
to change. This initiative strengthens 
Vedanta's reputation as an employer 
of choice in the manufacturing 
sector, reinforces the Group's 
target of 30% women workforce 
representation by FY 2029-30, and 
builds the cultural credibility that 
attracts and retains diverse talent 
across all operations.
What does this project do? 
Vedanta Aluminium has deployed 
a dedicated all-women team to 
manage the locomotive engine 
responsible for the internal 
movement of raw materials at its 
world-class aluminium smelter 
in Jharsuguda, Vedanta Group's 
largest aluminium plant. The 
team comprises four loco drivers 
operating in shifts, one gatewoman, 
and two support staff, collectively 
responsible for the efficient and safe 
operation and maintenance of this 
critical logistics asset.
Case Study 
This initiative is part of a broader, 
structured effort to open all 
operational roles to women across 
the plant. It follows a series of 
industry-first interventions at 
Jharsuguda, the launch of 'Shree 
Shakti', through which 108 women 
have taken on key operational roles 
during night shifts (a first in Odisha's 
industrial landscape), and the 
inauguration of the Indian aluminium 
industry's first all-women managed 
potline. The potline, a critical 
part of the aluminium production 
process, is being operationalised in 
three phases with more than 100 
women selected through internal 
job postings and upskilled through 
specialised training programmes.
Why is this project important?
The locomotive engine function sits 
at the core of plant logistics, without 
it, the movement of raw materials 
that feeds the entire smelting 
operation would stop. Placing 
women in charge of this function 
is a deliberate operational decision 
that reflects Vedanta Aluminium's 
conviction in gender-agnostic roles. 
In a country where women remain 
significantly underrepresented in 
mining, metals, and manufacturing, 
initiatives like this reshape what 
is perceived as possible for the 
women who take on these roles, for 
the colleagues who work alongside 
them, and for the next generation 
of women considering industrial 
careers. Vedanta Aluminium's 
approach also directly addresses 
a structural talent constraint: 
expanding the recruitment pool 
to include the full workforce, 
not half of it, produces stronger 
operational outcomes and greater 
organisational resilience.

roles as gender-agnostic from the

Economic Outlook
The year 2025-26 was marked by moderate 
and uneven global economic growth, as 
economies adjusted to increased trade 
protectionism, financial market volatility, and 
ongoing geopolitical uncertainties. While 
inflation eased and recession risks declined, 
structural challenges continued to shape the 
global outlook.
2025 – The Year of Uncertainty
The last fiscal started with President Donald 
Trump’s sweeping "Liberation Day" tariffs 
announcements in April 2025 introducing a 
baseline 10% global tariff alongside specific 
"reciprocal" tariffs scaling up to 50% for 
countries with high trade surpluses. This was 
followed by a series of negotiations, multiple 
changes in tariff rates and heightened trade 
tensions among the countries as they attempted 
to make trade deals with the US to achieve a 
favourable tariff structure. However, in February 
2026, the US Supreme Court ruled the initial 
tariffs illegal, stating that the emergency 
powers cited under the International Emergency 
Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) did not permit 
the President to bypass Congress to regulate 
international commerce. In response to the 
Supreme Court's decision, the US administration 
instituted a 10% blanket global tariff under 
Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which was 
again ruled out by the U.S. Court of International 
Trade (CIT) in May 2026.
The year was marked by increased number of 
conflicts amidst failed attempts to end Russia-
Ukraine war and fragile ceasefire in Gaza. New 
frontier opened in Middle East when the US, 
Israel and Iran engaged into the 12-Day War 
intensive conflict in June 2025 involving Israeli 
strikes on Iranian military and nuclear sites, 
followed by direct U.S. intervention.
Towards the end of the fiscal year, the fierce war 
broke out in Middle East between Iran and the 
US-Israel which rattled global energy market.
All these things culminated in heightened 
uncertainty regarding global business 
environment which is reflected in World 
Uncertainty Index which touched all-time high 
in September 2025, dwarfing the previous 
spikes like Covid-19 pandemic of 2020 or Global 
Financial Crisis of 2008.
Resilient Global Economy
Despite all the odds, global economy expanded by 3.4% 
in 2025, indicating stable but modest expansion. Growth 
remained strong in emerging economies which grew by 4.4%, 
but moderate in advanced economies with 1.9% rise in 2025. 
The United States maintained steady growth of 2.1% driven by 
consumption and technology investment. China managed to 
achieve the target 5% growth, supported by policy measures 
but constrained by real estate issues. India remained one 
of the fastest-growing major economies at 7.6%. Euro Area 
saw slower growth of 1.4% due to structural weaknesses. 
Overall, global growth was resilient but remained below 
long‑term averages.
Pace of decline in inflation slowed down in 2025 and global 
inflation largely remained steady. Inflation in the US remained 
above target level while that in India and EU started moving 
up during Q4 of FY 2025-26. As a result, the Federal Reserve 
kept its benchmark interest rate unchanged at 3.50–3.75% 
during meetings in January, March, and April in 2026 while 
the European Central Bank did not reduce interest rates after 
June 2025.
Global manufacturing in 2025 experienced a slow but steady 
recovery, characterised by moderate output growth. Global 
manufacturing PMI consistently remained in expansionary 
zone since August 2025 and reached 52.6 in April 2026 - 
marking a 49-month high and signalling a strengthened 
expansion in worldwide manufacturing output despite rising 
geopolitical risks. Global trade in 2025 reached a record high 
of US$ 34.65 trillion in total value, a 7% increase over 2024. 
Growth was driven by strong demand for electronics and 
AI-related hardware. However, sustenance of such positive 
developments are overshadowed by the ongoing war between 
Iran and the combined forces of US and Israel.

Middle East Crisis Risks Global Growth 
Prospect
The US-Iran war which started since 28 February 2026 has 
emerged as a major geopolitical shock with wide-ranging 
consequences for the global economy. Given the strategic 
importance of the Middle East in global energy supply and 
trade routes, the conflict has affected growth, inflation, trade, 
and financial stability worldwide.
The most immediate impact has been a sharp rise in global 
oil prices. The conflict disrupted the Strait of Hormuz, 
through which about 20% of global oil supply flows. Oil 
prices surged above US$ 100 per barrel in some phases. 
Rising oil and commodity prices have led to global inflation 
pressures. Many economies face the risk of imported 
inflation due to energy dependence. Higher cost of living 
(fuel, food, utilities), reduced purchasing power, pressure on 
low-income households.
Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz have 
impacted several commodity markets, affecting both energy 
and related sectors. The Gulf region, which accounts for 
about 8% of global aluminium supply, is also affected. 
Roughly 5 million tonnes are shipped annually through 
the Strait from countries like Bahrain, Qatar, Saudi Arabia, 
and the UAE, impacting construction, manufacturing, and 
energy technologies.
Fertiliser supply is especially vulnerable, with over 30% 
of global urea trade and around 20% of ammonia and 
phosphate shipments passing through the Strait. This raises 
concerns for food prices and security. There are also indirect 
energy implications, as some countries rely on imported 
LNG to power fertiliser production.
In addition, nearly half of global seaborne sulphur trade 
moves through this route. Sulphuric acid derived from it is 
essential for fertilisers, chemicals, petroleum refining, and 
processing key minerals such as copper, nickel, and zinc.
Oil and gas prices almost doubled and aluminium price 
also jumped due to supply disruption in Q4. While copper 
and silver prices reached all-time high earlier in the quarter, 
they retreated in the later part of the quarter due to profit 
booking, strengthening US dollar, fear of interest rate hike 
and concern of adverse impact of manufacturing.
The United States and Iran agreed to a fragile, two-week 
ceasefire on 8 April 2026, following which oil and gas prices 
pulled back. However, the ceasefire is currently in a state 
of tension following the failure of high-stakes negotiations. 
Resumption of the war and continuation of that may keep 
the commodity market extremely volatile.
Global Economic Outlook
The demand outlook has weakened as the conflict in the 
Middle East has disrupted fuel supplies, which will take time 
to recover once the Strait of Hormuz is fully reopened. But 
even that will not lead to a speedy return to normal as oil 
and gas production facilities and infrastructure have been 
damaged. As such, the fallout from the conflict could be 
felt for many months as it will take time for other producers 
to increase production to make up for the lasting losses in 
incurred by the affected Middle Eastern countries.
Central banks face a policy dilemma as inflation is likely to 
rise due to oil shocks while growth slowing due to economic 
uncertainty. This could delay interest rate cuts and 
possible tightening if inflation persists. This creates risks 
of stagflation which is a condition of low growth and high 
inflation, slower growth, and financial instability.
World industrial production growth for 2026 has been 
revised down from 3.1% to 2.5% as a result of the fallout 
of the conflict. With Asia and Europe highly dependent on 
Middle East oil and gas, higher-for-longer energy prices, 
energy rationing and the inflationary implications of these, 
means that there is a risk that broader markets turn bearish 
and that weighs on sentiment in the base metals.
In the baseline outlook by IMF, global growth is expected 
to reach 3.1% in 2026 and 3.2% in 2027. This represents a 
slowdown from the roughly 3.4% pace observed in 2024‑25, 
with growth stabilising at a similarly lower rate over the 
medium term – well below the historical average of 3.7% 
recorded between 2000 and 2019. Compared with the 
January 2026 WEO Update, the 2026 forecast has been 
revised down by 0.2 percentage points, while the 2027 
projection remains unchanged. Meanwhile, global headline 
inflation is projected to rise to 4.4% in 2026 before easing to 
3.7% in 2027, with both figures revised upward.
In a downside scenario characterised by larger and more 
sustained increases in energy prices, global growth would 
weaken further to 2.5% in 2026, while inflation would climb 
to 5.4%. Under a more severe scenario involving greater 
damage to energy infrastructure in the conflict-affected 
region, the consequences would intensify: global growth 
would fall to around 2% in 2026, and headline inflation 
would exceed 6% by 2027. Emerging market and developing 
economies would bear a disproportionately larger burden, 
experiencing impacts nearly twice as severe as those faced 
by advanced economies.
China
China's economy in 2025 achieved 5% growth, driven 
by robust manufacturing and exports despite persistent 
deflationary pressures, a prolonged property slump, and 
weak domestic demand.
In industrial sector, high-tech manufacturing outpaced the 
overall growth rate, with significant expansion in sectors like 
civil drones, embedded intelligence, and industrial robots. 
Fixed assets investments (FAI) registered a negative growth 
of 3.8% in 2025 – first time since 1989, mainly dragged 
down by 17% degrowth in investment in real estate sector. 
China's "anti-involution" drive to curb "race-to-the-bottom" 
competition, overcapacity, and destructive price wars, 
particularly in manufacturing also severely impacted FAI in 
manufacturing which could merely grew by 0.6% in 2025. 
Depressive situation in property market extended in 2025 
as well with 12.6% decline in building sold which calls for 
more structured and extended policy support from the 
Chinese government.
In March 2026, China adopted 15th Five-Year Plan 
(2026‑2030) which focusses on technological self-reliance, 
"new quality productive forces," and security-driven 
development. It sets a pragmatic 2026 GDP growth target 
of 4.5-5.0%. This shift prioritises high-quality development, 
technological self-reliance (AI, quantum computing), and 
service-sector growth over rapid speed. China has also 
stepped up efforts to launch major projects and boost 
investment in new types of infrastructure. The plan aims 
to manage domestic structural adjustments and weak 
demand, marking the lowest target in decades.
IMF has projected China’s GDP growth to decelerate to 4.4% 
in 2026 and 4% in 2027 from 5% in 2025 due to ongoing 
structural issues, specifically a prolonged property sector 
downturn, weak domestic consumption, an ageing labour 
force, and mounting trade tensions.

USA
The U.S. economy in 2025 showed steady and broad-
based growth – growing by 2.1%. This was driven mainly 
by strong consumer spending, a robust labour market, and 
AI-led technological investment. Despite challenges from 
high interest rates and global risks, the economy remained 
resilient and one of the strongest among advanced nations. 
Household consumption remained the largest driver of 
GDP, supported by strong labour market, rising wages and 
excess savings from previous years. US unemployment 
rate remained at 4.3% by the end of April 2026. But inflation 
rate jumped to 3.8% in April from 2.4% during January and 
February 2026 from rising energy cost.
US Fed adopted a cautious, data-dependent approach to 
interest rates in 2026, balancing inflation risks with concerns 
about economic growth due to ongoing Middle East war and 
rising fuel cost. As of early 2026, the Fed has kept the federal 
funds rate at 3.50%–3.75%. The Fed’s “dot plot” indicates 
only one rate cut in 2026 of 25 basis points, indicating a 
cautious "higher-for-longer" stance.
In February 2026, the U.S. Supreme Court ruled that 
President Trump's tariffs, imposed under the International 
Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA), were unlawful, 
ruling that only Congress has the authority to set import 
taxes. However, Donald Trump immediately activated 
Section 122 of the Trade Act of 1974, which allows for a 
temporary 15% general tariff to handle balance-of-payments 
issues. A 10% general tariff was subsequently slated to take 
effect by 24 February 2026, which is temporary (150 days) 
without Congressional approval.
The US economy is likely to be least affected by the Middle 
East war. IMF expects US GDP to grow by 2.3% in 2026 and 
2.1% in 2027.
European Union
The European Union's real GDP increased by 1.6% in 2025. 
This represented an acceleration from the 1.2% growth 
recorded in 2024. Economic performance varied significantly 
across the bloc, with smaller and island nations generally 
outpacing larger economies. Domestic demand remained 
a primary driver, supported by a resilient labour market and 
real wage increases as inflation cooled. Inflation stabilised 
around 2.1% for the year, significantly lower than previous 
peaks, which helped restore consumer purchasing power. 
As a result, ECB kept interest rates unchanged at 2.15% 
since June 2025. Manufacturing activities considerably 
improved as reflected in PMI reading which moved up to 
52 in April 2026.
However, the war in the Middle East has brought renewed 
uncertainty and the economic outlook is clouded again. 
Disruptions to shipping through the Strait of Hormuz, a key 
route for global oil and liquefied natural gas (LNG) trade. 
The baseline projections of IMF foresee annual real GDP 
growth of 1.3% in 2026 and 1.4% in 2027 and gas price-led 
cost push weighs on cost of living.

India’s economy stayed resilient in 2025-26, with real GDP 
growth of 7.6% under the Second Advance Estimates (base

consumption and fixed investment, while net external 
demand remained weak. On the supply side, real GVA rose 
7.7%, supported by robust services and manufacturing.
However, the ongoing conflict has increased volatility in 
global energy and commodity prices, creating uncertainty 
for the near-term growth and inflation outlook of India. 
Roughly 45% of crude oil and 60% of natural gas imports of 
India originate from the Middle East, making India’s energy 
security highly vulnerable to regional conflicts and shipping 
disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. Higher global energy 
costs have pushed up prices of fuels like premium petrol, 
LPG, and industrial diesel.
The Indian rupee hit an all-time low of 95.75 against the US 
Dollar on 14 May 2026, driven by intense pressures from 
the Middle East conflict, surging oil prices, and significant 
foreign capital outflows.
Indian domestic industries also initially experienced 
disruptions due to constrained availability of natural gas, 
as the Indian government had prioritised natural gas and 
LPG allocation to households and transport over industrial 
users following supply disruptions in the Strait of Hormuz. 
Subsequently, government gradually increased the allocation 
of bulk non-domestic LPG to industrial sectors closure to 
their pre-March 2026 consumption levels.
The Government of India has launched several emergency 
measures to support domestic industries and exporters 
facing disruptions due to the US-Iran conflict and related 
volatility in West Asia.
	•
The RELIEF Scheme: The Ministry of Commerce and 
Industry introduced the ` 497 crore RELIEF (Resilience & 
Logistics Intervention for Export Facilitation) scheme to 
mitigate rising freight and insurance costs for exporters 
targeting 10 West Asian countries. It assists exporters 
facing high freight costs, rising insurance premiums, and 
logistics delays in West Asia, covering regions like the 
UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and expanding to include Egypt 
and Jordan.
	
– Risk Coverage: ECGC Ltd. (Formerly Export Credit 
Guarantee Corporation of India Ltd.) offers up to 
100% risk coverage over and above the existing ECGC 
cover for existing policies from 14 February 2026 till 
15 March 2026 and 95% for new shipments between 
14 February and 15 June 2026, keeping premiums at 
pre-conflict rates.
	
– MSME Support: Provides up to 50% reimbursement 
(capped at ` 50 lakhs) for extraordinary shipping/
insurance surcharges.
	•
Restoration of Duty Benefits: Government fully restored 
RoDTEP (Remission of Duties and Taxes on Exported 
Products) rates and value caps till  30 September 
2026 for the benefit of exporters, reversing a February 
reduction of 50%.
	•
Logistical Support: Govt launched US$ 1.5 billion Bharat 
Maritime Insurance Pool with sovereign guarantee to 
secure shipping risks.
Looking ahead to 2026-27, high energy and commodity 
prices and potential supply disruptions (e.g., Strait of 
Hormuz) may weigh on production. Global financial volatility 
and trade disruptions could also impact growth, especially 
exports due to higher shipping and insurance costs. 
However, strong services momentum, GST rationalisation, 
rising manufacturing capacity use, and healthy corporate 
and financial balance sheets should support demand. With 
government initiatives to boost domestic manufacturing, 
GDP growth is projected at 6.9% (Q1: 6.8%, Q2: 6.7%, 
Q3: 7.0%, Q4: 7.2%) by RBI, higher than 6.5% projected 
by IMF. Risks remain from prolonged conflict, wider 
geopolitical tensions, energy infrastructure damage, and 
weather shocks.
Taking these factors into account, CPI inflation for 2026-27 
is projected at 4.6% (Q1: 4.0%, Q2: 4.4%, Q3: 5.2%, Q4: 4.7%). 
Upside risks remain due to persistently high energy prices 
from the West Asia conflict and potential El Niño conditions 
that could affect the southwest monsoon.

Aluminium
Market Overview
The aluminium market on the 
LME witnessed considerable 
price fluctuations in FY 2025-26. 
In April 2025, aluminium prices 
were US$ 2,381 per tonne, rising to 
US$ 2,600/t levels in July due to 50% 
tariffs imposed by USA in June 2025. 
LME maintained steady uptrend 
till January 2026 rising to ~3,150/t 
levels due to various factors; China’s 
production nearing the production 
cap of 45 MTPA, weakening of US 
Dollar, & frequent variations in tariffs 
from USA. The middle east conflict 
led smelter shutdowns propelled 
LME prices to multi-year highs of 
~3,400 US$/t during March.
In CY 2025, global primary 
aluminium production was ~1.1% 
up from last year and around 
73.8 million tonnes. The demand 
was also around at the same level 
with deficit balance of ~0.2 million. 
In the world excluding China, both 
production and consumption were at 
similar levels as per last year. China’s 
production increased in CY 2025 
was 44.2 MTPA. In India, the demand 
surged by ~10% to around 6 million 
tonnes in FY 2025-26.
Market Outlook
The global demand for aluminium 
is anticipated to increase at a 
CAGR of ~2.5% from 2025 to 
2030. Decarbonisation initiatives 
and a transition away from 
fossil fuels in the transportation 
sector will see an increase in 
aluminium consumption up to 
~32 million tonnes by 2030. The 
demand for renewable energy 
will drive an increased demand 
for aluminium for solar panel 
manufacturing, transmission & 
distribution and the replacement 
of existing copper wiring in power 
distribution systems.
China, the world's largest 
aluminium consumer, shows 
promising signs of continued 
domestic consumption growth. 
However, its long-term success 
hinges on sustained growth in 
the transportation sector and 
modest recovery of the building 
& construction industry. For 
the Rest of the World, 2026 is 
expected to experience volatile 
market due to macroeconomic 
conditions like tariffs from 
USA, and geopolitical situations 
impacting trade flow & fuel and 
commodity prices and decrease 
in global production capacity due 
to expected shutdown of South32 
Aluminium Smelter (Mozal) from 
March 2026.
Meanwhile, India stands out 
with its robust domestic 
demand outlook of more than 
8% growth for FY 2026-27. Key 
sectors like electrical industry, 
automotive, and anticipated 
growth in renewables, defence 
and aerospace will continue to 
drive aluminium consumption in 
the country.
Products and Customers
Vedanta is India’s largest 
primary aluminium producer 
with an annual capacity of ~2.4 
million tonnes. The Company’s 
product portfolio includes 
aluminium ingots, primary 
foundry alloys, wire rods, billets, 
and rolled products which cater 
to varied industries globally 
such as energy, transportation, 
construction and packaging, 
aerospace and defence, among 
others. It has achieved domestic 
market share of 46%.
In line with the evolving market 
needs and the focus on value 
creation through expanding 
margins, the Company has 
been steadily increasing its 
value‑added product (VAP) share 
in the portfolio which currently 
accounts for ~60% of its total 
global aluminium sales and 
targeting ~90%.

High Carbon 
Ferro Chrome
Market Overview
High Carbon Ferro Chrome 
(HCFC) is pivotal to the global 
stainless-steel industry, 
enhancing its non-corrosive, 
durable, and temperature-
resistant qualities. Over 
85% of HCFC production is 
dedicated to stainless steel 
manufacturing, indicating that 
a flourishing stainless-steel 
sector is a bellwether for strong 
HCFC demand.
Asia, with China at the 
helm, dominates the HCFC 
landscape, accounting for 85% 
of consumption and holding 
substantial chromite ore reserves, 
the essential raw material. 
Although South Africa is the 
premier chromite ore supplier 
worldwide, China’s leadership 
in HCFC production positions it 
as a dominant force in shaping 
global market dynamics and 
pricing structures.
India is playing a significant role 
in the HCFC market, securing 
the position as the world’s 
fourth-largest producer with an 
output of ~1.2 million tonnes in 
CY 2025. India’s HCFC market 
is characterised by an export 
orientation, with ~55% of its 
production being exported.
In Q4 FY 2025-26, Ferro chrome 
prices peaked at ` 1,24,000/T 
highest levels since September 
2023. Demand in Q1 FY 2026-27 is 
primarily driven by exports which 
is supported by the exchange 
rate making exports much more 
lucrative as the domestic demand 
is expected to pick up gradually 
trailing the robust stainless 
steel prices.
Market Drivers
With India’s solid domestic market 
and the anticipated global upswing 
in stainless steel production, the 
outlook for HCFC is optimistic. 
With increasing infrastructure 
initiatives in developing nations 
and an expected resurgence in 
demand from China, stainless steel 
production is projected to grow 
steadily by 4-5% in the upcoming 
year. This growth trajectory is set to 
catalyse HCFC demand worldwide, 
with production forecasts 
suggesting an increase of 3-4%.
India, however, is on track to 
surpass the global growth rate, 
emerging as the fastest-expanding 
market for both stainless steel 
and HCFC production. The 
projected 7-8% growth in Stainless 
Steel sector is propelled by the 
Indian government’s substantial 
investment in infrastructure 
development. Moreover, India’s per 
capita consumption of stainless 
steel is poised for a significant 
uptick, mirroring the expanding 
domestic HCFC market.
Company Overview
Ferro Alloys Corporation (FACOR) 
stands out in the domestic 
HCFC sector, ranking as the 
fourth-largest supplier amidst a 
predominantly export-oriented 
industry. In FY 2025-26, FACOR 
channelled almost all of its HCFC 
production to meet the needs of 
domestic stainless steel and alloy 
steel manufacturers.
Getting future-ready along 
with expansion, FACOR is also 
strategically augmenting its Value-
Added Products (VAP) portfolio, 
thereby securing a competitive 
edge to serve specialised markets 
in Europe and South Korea. 
Looking forward to FY 2026-27, 
FACOR’s strategy is geared towards 
amplifying production volumes and 
expanding its market presence, 
both domestically and globally.
At our Ferroalloy business, our 
strategic emphasis remains 
on capacity expansion, 
prioritising domestic market, 
VAP development, and strategic 
international market expansion. We 
are ideally positioned to thrive in 
this dynamic market landscape.
Oil
Global Oil Market Overview
In 2025, the global oil supply 
experienced moderate growth, 
primarily driven by both non-OPEC 
nations such as the United States 
(+0.76 Mb/d), Brazil (+0.37 Mb/d), 
Canada (+0.26 Mb/d), Kazakhstan 
(+0.27 Mb/d), China, and OPEC 
nations like Saudi Arabia (+0.49 
Mb/d), UAE and Venezuela. Global 
oil demand also saw an upward 
trend, increasing by approximately 
1.14 Mb/d. Sustained economic 
growth across Asia, driven by 
continued expansion in China, 
India, and other non‑OECD 
countries, has been the primary 
catalyst for rising oil demand, 
fuelled largely by increasing 
transportation and industrial fuel 
consumption in these regions.
India's oil demand in 2025 
rose to 5.65 Mb/d (+0.1 Mb/d). 
It maintained strong growth driven 
by robust private consumption 
following GST reductions and 
sustained government spending. 
Monetary easing through rate 
cuts further supported growth 
momentum, though labour market 
pressures persisted.
Crude oil prices in 2025 averaged 
US$ 69.1 per barrel, marking a 
14.5% decline from 2024. Monthly 
prices trended broadly downwards 
from US$ 79.2 in January to US$ 
62.7 by year end, with a brief spike 
in June–July due to the US Iran 
conflict. The overall decline was 
driven by the unwinding of OPEC+ 
voluntary cuts and abundant 
supply from outside the group 
causing a supply glut. OPEC+ 
began reversing the reductions 
made in 2023 by fully restoring 
2.2 mb/d of output by September 
and partially rolling back the 
remaining 1.65 mb/d later in the 
year. Despite this oversupply, 
geo-political events like Middle 
East conflict led to sudden spike in 
crude oil price to over US$ 100/bbl 
since March 2026.
Market Drivers
OPEC forecasts global oil demand 
will grow by 1.4 Mb/d to reach 
106.5 Mb/d in 2026. This increase 
will be driven by strong air travel 
demand, greater road mobility, 
including on-road diesel and 
trucking, and robust industrial, 
construction, and agricultural 
activities, particularly in non-OECD 
nations. Non-OECD production 
is expected to rise by 0.4 Mb/d in 
2026, with growth led by the Latin 
American region (+0.4 Mb/d). 
Geopolitical factors, including the 
ongoing Middle East conflict and 
trade tariffs, could significantly 
impact global oil supply.
Brent crude oil prices have surged 
sharply following the outbreak 
of military conflict in the Middle 
East, rising more than 50% since 
the start of 2026. The U.S. Energy 
Information Administration (EIA) 
projects that Brent will average 
around US$ 79 per barrel in 2026, 
as the effective closure of the Strait 
of Hormuz temporarily reduces 
Middle Eastern oil production. 
Prices are expected to remain 
elevated through the second 
quarter of 2026, before easing 
below US$ 80 per barrel in the third 
quarter as production gradually 
resumes with the reopening of 
the Strait.
Manufacturing, business activity, 
air travel, and road mobility are 
expected to stay steady, while 
government initiatives such as 
Make in India, GST reforms, and 
the PMUY scheme will boost 
local demand. Strong GDP growth 
is also likely to sustain internal 
combustion engine vehicle sales 
amid slow EV penetration, pointing 
to a positive near‑term outlook 
for oil product demand which is 
forecast to increase by 0.23 Mb/d 
to 5.9 Mb/d in 2026.
Products and Customers
Cairn Oil & Gas, is one of the largest 
private oil and gas exploration 
and production companies in 
the country, has gross proven 
and probable reserves and 
resources of 1,321 million barrels 
of oil equivalent (mmboe). The 
company’s crude oil is sold to both 
public and private refineries, while 
its natural gas is consumed by the 
city gas distribution, fertiliser, and 
other industrial sectors in India.
In FY 2025-26, 100% of the 
company’s crude oil and natural 
gas production was sold within 
India, in accordance with 
government regulations.

Power Sector
Demand and Supply
India's power sector witnessed 
significant advancements in 
FY 2025-26, highlighted by a record 
peak power demand of 245 GW, met 
with resilience and improved energy 
infrastructure. India's power sector 
has shown strong growth, with 
electricity generation 1,830 billion 
units in FY 2024-25 and 1,848 billion 
units in FY 2025-26, witnessing 1% 
Y-o-Y growth. Capacity additions 
were robust at 12%, bringing total 
installed capacity to 533 GW in 
FY 2025-26 compared to 475 GW 
in FY 2024-25. Notable strides were 
made in renewable energy, with an 
additional 55 GW capacity added in 
FY 2025‑26, and 7G W coal-based 
plant capacity addition in same 
period to meet rising demand. 
As per CEA, India is projected to 
witness coal (including lignite) 
installed capacity requirement of 
291 GW by FY 2031-32 to meet 
round the clock power demand.
With initiatives like universal 
electrification, improved rural 
power availability, and enhanced 
energy conservation efforts, India 
is on a robust path to becoming a 
global energy leader.
Market drivers
India's power sector is 
experiencing rapid growth, driven 
by several key macroeconomic 
factors. As per World Economic 
Forum, the country's population 
is projected to reach 1.515 
billion by 2030, with urbanisation 
accelerating the demand for 
electricity. Notably, India's per 
capita electricity consumption has 
surged to 1,460 kWh in 2024-25, 
which is estimated to reach 2,000 
kWh by 2030 and 4,000 kWh 
by 2047.
For the year 2035-36 India has set 
an ambitious electricity generation 
target of 3596 billion units, 
reflecting a 95% increase from the 
1,848 billion units generated in the 
2025-26. The 2025-26 generation 
mix includes 1,307 billion units 
from thermal power, 175 billion 
units from solar power, 167 billion 
units from large hydro power and 
55 billion units from nuclear.
Fossil Fuel based plants, 
primarily fueled by coal and 
lignite, now account for 249 GW 
of installed capacity, making up 
46.8% of the total generation 
capacity. Meanwhile, non-
fossil fuel sources, such as 
renewable energy and nuclear 
power, contribute 283 GW of 
installed capacity.
In India, rural average daily supply 
increased from 12.5 hours in 
FY 2013-14 to 22.6 hours in 
FY 2024-25, while urban areas 
also saw improvement, with daily 
average supply rising from 22.1 
hours to 23.4 hours over the same 
period. This highlights significant 
progress in the reliability 
and reach of the country’s 
electricity infrastructure.
Round-the-clock (RTC) tariffs 
for power in the Day Ahead 
Market (DAM) for FY 2025-26 are 
set at ₹ 3.8 per kWh, reflecting 
ongoing stability in the power 
pricing landscape
Products and consumers
Vedanta Power is strategically 
positioned to capitalise on the 
expanding power market. With 
operational merchant thermal 
power capacity of 4.2 GW, the 
company is 5th largest private 
thermal player. Key assets include 
Talwandi Sabo Thermal Plant 
(1,980 MW), Sakti Thermal Plant 
(600 MW operational, 600 MW

Q2FY 2025‑26. Vedanta Power

with TNPDCL, of which Meenakshi 
Energy secured 300 MW and Sakti 
Thermal Plant secured 200 MW. The 
mix of Merchant and PPA power 
supply in these newly commissioned 
units provide Vedanta Power with 
a blend of secured revenue and 
maximisation of market rates.
Vedanta Power secured 5.34 million 
metric tonnes of linkage coal for 
the new assets, Meenakshi Energy

Thermal Plant (2.7 million metric 
tonnes).
MEL is strategically located near to

Zinc
Market Overview
In FY 2025-26, the zinc price 
stayed buoyant, touching peak 
of US$ 3,487 per tonne, the 
highest level since February 
2023, and averaging at US$ 2,970 
per tonne, a 3% Y-o-Y increase. 
The rally was supported by tight 
physical inventories and strong 
consumption in galvanising and 
infrastructure segments, alongside 
rising geopolitical concerns and a 
weakening dollar.
In CY 2024-25, global zinc demand 
surged by 0.6% Y-o-Y to 13.66 Mnt, 
driven by rapid urbanisation, 
renewable energy (RE) transition, 
and structural consumption drivers 
in end-use markets. In China, the 
demand was weighed down by 
weak real estate, partially offset 
by growth in automotive and 
appliances. Europe witnessed 
2% consumption growth as auto 
production stabilised despite 
sluggish construction. In the US, 
steady steel mill utilisation, tariff 
developments, and firm non-
residential construction supported 
galvanised steel demand, with a 
potential upside from continued 
steel and auto sector momentum.
Market Outlook
Galvanising is the dominant zinc 
application, accounting for 60% of 
the total use driven by its critical 
role in construction, transport, and 
infrastructure. These diverse and 
critical end-uses reinforce zinc’s 
relevance and resilience across 
economic cycles.
India remained a major global 
driver of zinc demand, with 
consumption rising from 814 kt 
in CY 2024 to 851 kt in CY 2025, 
supported by broad industrial 
and infrastructure growth. 
This was reflected in the India 
Manufacturing Purchasing 
Managers’ Index (PMI), averaging 
around 58 in CY 2026, and Index 
of Industrial Production (IIP), 
peaking in December 2025 with 
a growth of 7.8%, translating into 
higher demand for galvanised 
steel, zinc alloys, castings 
and chemicals.
Government programmes such 
as Gati Shakti and the National 
Infrastructure Pipeline, along with 
strong steel and cement demand, 
continue to sustain galvanising 
requirements across transport, 
power, housing, and utilities. 
Road and rail modernisation 
alone generates a large part 
of the demand for galvanised 
steel structures.
Recently, energy transition 
investments, including in solar 
and wind installations, power 
grid expansion, and transmission 
towers, have emerged as 
significant drivers of galvanised 
steel structures. Simultaneously, 
rising auto and appliance 
production continue to boost 
demand for galvanised structures 
and zinc die cast components, 
with emerging applications 
in zinc-based batteries and 
specialised zinc products. 
Favourable trade dynamics 
and new export opportunities 
are further reinforcing India’s 
role as a strategic zinc supply hub, 
supporting smelter throughput and 
domestic availability.
Market Outlook
As per Wood Mackenzie, global zinc 
demand in CY 2026 is expected to grow 
at 1% Y-o-Y to 13.80 Mnt, supported 
by marginal increases in China, 
stabilising European consumption, and 
a stronger US steel linked demand. 
Mine supply is expected to remain tight, 
with output projected to fall by 4.1% 
Y-o-Y to 12.39 Mnt due to significant 
production cuts and the absence of 
major new project additions, resulting 
in consistently low treatment charges. 
Prices are forecast to average at c.US$ 
3,064 per tonne in CY 2026, supported 
by low refined stocks and a softer US 
dollar, before gradually easing towards 
US$ 2,800 per tonne from CY 2026-27 
onwards as refined stocks accumulate 
due to increased utilisation of China’s 
new smelting capacity.
Over the medium term, the global 
mine output is expected to plateau 
by CY 2028 and begin declining from 
CY 2029 onwards as the pipeline of 
advanced stage projects remains thin.
India and Southeast Asia are expected 
to account for the bulk of incremental 
demand for refined zinc. With India 
targeting 300 Mnt of crude steel 
capacity by 2030, aligned with the 
National Steel Policy and long‑term 
sectoral growth plans, the domestic 
zinc demand is forecasted to grow 
proportionately. This provides a strong 
foundation for our ambitious growth 
plan to double capacity.
Company Overview
Hindustan Zinc, the world’s largest 
integrated zinc producer and India’s 
only primary zinc manufacturer, held 
a 74% domestic primary market share 
in FY 2025-26 with 600 kt of domestic 
zinc sales. Value-Added Products 
(VAP) stood at 184 kt, contributing 
to c.22% of total sales. Around 70% 
of refined zinc was sold within the 
domestic market, while 30% was 
exported to South East Asia, the 
Middle East, the US, and Europe.
We continued to progress towards 
our ambition of 100% online price 
discovery (OPD) sales, achieving 
95% OPD sales in FY 2025-26. The 
launch of Zinc Moolya, a rupee-linked 
live pricing module in January 2026, 
further enhanced price transparency 
and simplified transactions for 
micro, small and medium enterprises 
(MSMEs).
FY 2025-26 marked a breakthrough 
year for commercial scaling of EcoZen, 
Asia’s first low carbon zinc brand with 
a carbon footprint of less than 1 tCO2e 
per tonne. We signed Memorandums 
of Understanding (MoUs) with Tata 
Steel and Silox India Limited and 
delivered EcoZen, reinforcing efforts 
to accelerate its adoption across 
galvanising operations.
We signed MoUs with CMR Group 
and Tripura Group to operationalise 
manufacturing units at our upcoming 
Zinc Park in Khankhala, Rajasthan. 
These collaborations represent a key 
step towards building India’s first 
integrated downstream hub for zinc 
based industries that is scalable, 
efficient and sustainable, supported 
by assured raw material linkage and 
long-term offtake commitments. 
This initiative will help attract 
new investments, foster MSME 
growth, generate local employment, 
and accelerate Make in India 
manufacturing near our operations at 
Chanderiya, Dariba and Debari.

Lead
Market Overview
Lead prices softened during 
FY 2025-26, averaging at 
US$ 1,954 per tonne and settling 
below US$ 1,900 per tonne. This 
was due to adequate supply in 
the market rather than weakening 
demand. In CY 2025, global 
refined lead production increased 
by 1% to 14.35 Mnt, while primary 
mine output increased by 3.4% to 
4.44 Mnt.
In CY 2025, global refined lead 
demand surged by 0.5% Y-o-Y to 
14.24 Mnt. This was mainly driven 
by strong automotive battery 
demand across both original 
equipment manufacturers and 
replacement markets, expansion 
in stationary battery applications 
across data centres, telecom and 
grid storage, and robust growth 
in Asia.
Lead demand continues to be 
anchored in starting-lighting-
ignition (SLI) and auxiliary 
batteries across global internal 
combustion engines (ICE) and 
hybrid fleets, as well as energy 
storage and backup power 
applications. Factors like rising 
hybrid registrations in Europe, 
regulatory tightening on low 
voltage lithium ion batteries in 
China, and sustained growth in 
two- and three-wheeler mobility 
and telecom/backup power 
applications in India continue 
to reinforce its demand. Its 
recyclability of over 95% makes 
enhances its sustainability profile, 
while its role in enabling cost-
effective, large-scale energy 
storage supports RE integration 
and global energy security.
Market Outlook
India’s total lead consumption for 
FY 2025-26 stood at 1.36 Mnt, 
majorly driven by batteries, 
cables, and galvanisers, etc. 
Indian lead demand is supported 
by batteries for automotive 
and energy applications, 
with overall consumption 
increasing due to its wider 
use in SLI batteries, cable 
sheathing, and PVC stabilisers. 
It also finds application in 
sectors like defence systems, 
telecommunications, railways, 
logistics, and industrial 
backup power.
Global refined lead demand 
is projected to grow steadily 
by 2.2% Y-o-Y to 14.56 Mnt in 
CY 2026, supported by stable 
automotive and stationary 
battery applications. China’s 
refined lead demand is expected 
to reach 6.34 Mnt in CY 2026, 
supported by strong new energy 
vehicle (NEV) related battery 
exports and industrial use. 
Against this, the global primary 
mine output is expected to 
shrink by 4.1% Y-o-Y to 4.25 Mnt 
with limited new project 
additions keeping concentrate 
markets tight.
Company Overview
Hindustan Zinc strengthened 
its position as India’s leading 
lead producer, increasing its 
domestic primary market 
share to 90% in FY 2025-26, up 
from 74% in FY 2024-25. This 
was supported by long-term 
contracts with large battery 
manufacturers in India, which 
secured a stable and consistent 
offtake. Over 80% of our refined 
lead production, translating into 
157 kt was sold domestically, 
with 50 kt in exports. The 
production was focussed on 
99.99% purity lead ingots, 
registered with the London Metal 
Exchange, with efforts underway 
to optimise sales mix towards 
100% domestic consumption 
by securing new customers and 
enhancing lead applications.
Silver
Global demand and supply
Silver prices rallied to record 
highs during FY 2025-26, touching 
historic highs of US$ 118.45 per 
toz in January 2026, and averaging 
US$ 53.09 per toz, up 75% Y-o-Y. 
This spike was driven by record 
exchange traded product (ETP) 
inflows, record tight market 
conditions, and heightened tariff 
and policy uncertainty in the US. 
Further, strong physical/investment 
demand that re routed metal into US 
vaults while tightening availability 
in London, a compression of the 
gold‑to‑silver ratio below 72, and 
its new designation as a US critical 
mineral led to strategic stockpiling.
Silver demand is being structurally 
redefined by high-growth sectors 
such as AI infrastructure, 5G, and 
EV components. These emerging 
applications, alongside India’s 
massive bullion imports of over 
6,000 tonnes outstripped industrial 
substitution efforts. As a result, 
industrial fabrication hit a new all-
time high of c.700 Moz, offsetting 
the decline in photovoltaic demand 
caused by aggressive thrifting as 
manufacturers reacted to silver's 
price surge.
Global mine output remained 
stagnant at 813 Moz due 
to declining ore grades and 
operational challenges across 
mines. The market recorded its 
fifth consecutive deficit of 95 Moz 
in CY 2025 as total supply rose by 
only 1% Y-o-Y to 1,022 Moz, while 
demand reached 1,117 Moz. This 
persistent shortfall has resulted 
in a cumulative five-year deficit of 
over 820 Moz, severely depleting 
above-ground inventories.
Indian demand
India’s silver demand reached 
an exceptional high of 7,000 MT 
in CY 2025, underscoring the 
country’s position as the largest 
consumer of silver globally, 
with usage driven across 
industrial, investment, and 
fabrication sectors.
Domestic markets experienced 
notable tightness throughout 
CY 2025 due to strong technology 
linked consumption (solar 
manufacturing, EV production, 
electronics, and semiconductor), 
festive buying, and heavy investor 
accumulation. This resulted in 
periodic physical shortages as 
demand consistently outpaced 
available supply, while positioning 
silver as an essential material in 
India’s clean energy and high tech 
growth story.
Investor behaviour shifted 
dramatically towards silver, with 
buyers accumulating metal even 
at record high price levels. ETF 
inflows, bar and coin purchases, and 
minimal scrap selling highlighted 
strong confidence and created 
sustained upward pressure on 
physical demand.
Outlook
Global silver supply is forecasted 
to reach a decade high of 1.05 
billion ounces in CY 2026, up 
1.5% Y-o-Y, driven by a surge in 
recycling and a modest rise in mine 
output to 820 Moz. While Mexico 
remains the leading producer, a 
long-term decline towards 186 Moz 
is anticipated by CY 2029 due to 
maturing legacy assets.
	•
Total global demand remains 
structurally high but increasing 
diversified. While high prices may 
lead to thrifting and substitution 
in solar and electronics, yet this 
is expected to be offset by a 20% 
jump in physical investment and 
emerging industrial uses.
	•
The outlook is defined by a 
persistent physical tightness, 
as the market enters its sixth 
consecutive year of structural 
deficit, projected at 67 Moz. 
It sustains an optimistic 
environment where the metal’s 
dual role as a safe-haven hedge 
and a critical technology mineral 
has established a significantly 
higher price floor compared to 
previous years.
Company Overview
Hindustan Zinc is the only primary 
silver producer in India and is 
amongst the top 10 silver producers 
globally. Over the past two decades, 
we have delivered a remarkable 
20x growth in silver production, 
and its contribution towards overall 
profitability increased to c.45% 
in FY 2025-26. We showcased 
a robust sales performance of 
627 MT in FY 2025-26, with 100% 
sales in the domestic market.

Iron ore
Market Overview
The global iron ore market 
remained resilient during 
FY 2025-26, supported by steady 
steel production and sustained 
infrastructure investments across 
major emerging economies. While 
China's steel demand continued 
to face structural headwinds from 
the prolonged correction in its 
property sector, demand across 
India, Southeast Asia and other 
developing markets remained 
robust, helping offset weakness in 
mature economies.
According to the World Steel 
Association, global steel demand 
is expected to bottom out 
and return to modest growth, 
supported by public infrastructure 
spending, manufacturing 
investments and easing financial 
conditions. Developing economies, 
particularly India, continue 
to be the key drivers of steel 
consumption growth.
Iron ore prices remained volatile 
during the year, largely influenced 
by Chinese economic stimulus 
measures, inventory movements 
and global supply dynamics. 
Benchmark seaborne iron ore 
prices broadly traded around the 
US$ 90–110 per tonne range, 
reflecting the balancing effect 
of softer Chinese steel demand 
and resilient consumption across 
emerging markets.
Market Outlook
The medium-term outlook for 
iron ore remains constructive. 
Global steel demand is expected 
to gradually recover, supported 
by infrastructure-led growth, 
manufacturing investments and 
energy transition-related projects. 
While excess steelmaking capacity 
and trade-related uncertainties 
continue to pose challenges 
globally, India is expected to 
remain the most significant source 
of incremental steel and iron 
ore demand.
With sustained investments in 
roads, railways, urban infrastructure, 
renewable energy and industrial 
manufacturing, India is expected 
to play an increasingly pivotal role 
in shaping global steel and iron ore 
markets over the coming decade.
Company Overview
The Company has solidified its 
position as a key player in the 
production of iron ore and pig 
iron, serving the steelmaking, 
construction, and infrastructure 
industries. With a strategic focus on 
optimising its mining operations, the 
Company has achieved significant 
production milestones. Sesa Goa 
is one of the largest private sector 
exporters of iron ore in India. Our 
total iron ore saleable production 
through IOK and IOG Mines is 
6.5 million DMT, 5% up Y-o-Y. Pig 
iron production is at the highest 
levels with 895 kt production in 
FY 2025‑26.
Steel
Market Overview
India further strengthened its 
position as the world's second-
largest crude steel producer 
during FY 2025-26, with crude 
steel production reaching 
approximately 169 million tonnes, 
representing growth of over 
11% Y-o-Y.
Global steel markets remained 
challenged by excess capacity, 
weak demand in certain regions 
and continued exports from 
China. However, policy measures 
implemented by the Government 
of India helped moderate import 
pressures and support domestic 
producers. Following the 
imposition of safeguard measures 
on select steel imports, finished 
steel imports declined significantly 
during FY 2025-26, while exports 
recorded strong growth.
Market Outlook and Drivers
India’s steel demand is projected 
to remain robust, supported by 
sustained momentum across 
core consuming sectors such 
as infrastructure, construction, 
housing, automobiles and 
engineering. The World Steel 
Association forecasts a 9% 
annual growth in India’s steel 
consumption through 2025 
and 2026, driven primarily by 
large-scale public capex and 
accelerating urban development.
Further, the Union Cabinet’s recent 
decision to extend and restructure 
the Jal Jeevan Mission (JJM) until 
December 2028 with an enhanced 
outlay of ₹ 8.69 lakh crore –
strengthens demand visibility for 
DI pipes.
Company Overview
ESL Steel Limited or ESL is an 
integrated steel plant situated in 
Bokaro, Jharkhand, with a design 
hot metal capacity of 3.5 MTPA. 
Its current operating hot metal 
capacity is 1.5 MTPA with a 
diversified product portfolio of 
Wire Rod, Rebar, DI Pipe and Pig 
Iron which are sold across key 
sectors such as construction, 
infrastructure, transportation 
and energy.
ESL achieved hot metal production 
of 1.384 million tonnes down 3% 
Y-o-Y and saleable production 
of 1.301 million tonnes down 
3% Y-o-Y primarily due to the 
maintenance activities in one of 
the furnaces and subdued demand 
in the DI pipe segment. Also, ESL 
achieved the highest-ever annual 
production of Billet, TMT and Wire 
rod in the history of ESL.
The key strategic priority remains 
increasing our hot metal capacity 
from 1.5 MTPA to 3.5 MTPA by 
FY 2026-27 and downstream 
expansion in further years. This 
strategic capacity enhancement 
aligns with our vision to become 
a high grade, low cost steel 
producer, operating with the 
highest standards of environment, 
health and safety, while serving 
India’s growing requirement for 
quality steel products.

Operational Review 
ZINC INDIA
The year in brief
Zinc India is the world’s largest 
integrated zinc producer and 
amongst the Top 10 silver 
producers globally. During the 
year, the Company achieved a 
record mined metal production 
of 1,114 kt, driven by higher ore 
production and improved mined 
metal grades. Refined metal 
production stood at 1,048 kt, 
supported by the commissioning 
of debottlenecking projects and 
the 160 KTPA roaster, including 
a record refined zinc output of 
851 kt, up 3% Y-o-Y. Refined lead 
production was 197 kt, reflecting 
a 13% Y-o-Y decline, primarily 
due to prior-year pyro operations 
being partially in lead mode and 
lower plant availability. Refined 
silver production for the year was 
627 tonnes.
ESG Update
In August 2025, Hindustan Zinc achieved a historic 
milestone by becoming the 25th member of the International 
Council on Mining & Metals (ICMM), and notably, the first 
new entrant since 2021. With this achievement, Hindustan 
Zinc also became the first Indian company to get this 
prestigious membership, a moment of great significance 
for both the organisation and the Indian mining industry. 
As ICMM represents the global benchmark for responsible 
mining, encompassing leadership in social performance, 
environmental stewardship, safety, and ethical practices, 
the Company’s membership marks a transformative step 
that positions India prominently on the global stage of 
sustainable and responsible mining.
Furthermore, for the third consecutive year, Hindustan Zinc 
has been recognised as the global ESG leader in S&P Global 
Corporate Assessment 2025, being ranked 1st among 235 
companies globally in metals and mining sector. With 
an improvement in overall score to 90 out of 100, the 
Company also got featured in the Sustainability Yearbook 
2026 amongst the top 1% most sustainable organisations 
globally for the ninth consecutive year.
Occupational Health and Safety 
At Hindustan Zinc, ensuring the safety, health, and well-
being of our employees and business partners remains 
a core organisational priority. Guided by our 'Zero Harm' 
philosophy, we continue to strengthen systems, leadership 
accountability, and risk management practices to create 
a workplace where every individual returns home safely. 
However, during the year, we had two unfortunate fatalities 
in our operations.
Following detailed investigation, we implemented 
strong corrective and preventive measures with utmost 
urgency, and the learnings were disseminated across 
the organisation. The safety and well-being of every 
individual remain paramount, and these incidents serve 
as a reminder of the need for constant vigilance and 
continuous improvement. 
During the year, the Company reinforced its safety 
governance framework through enhanced risk management 
systems, leadership capability building, and structured 
engagement with employees and business partners.
A significant milestone during the year was the rollout 
of a Critical Risk Management (CRM) centric Safety 
Management System across operations. The CRM 
framework focusses on identifying high-consequence 
risks and ensuring the implementation of effective critical 
controls to prevent fatalities and serious incidents. As 
part of this programme, five additional critical risks were 
launched during FY 2025-26, including risks related to 
Heavy Earth Moving Machinery (HEMM) fire, ventilation 
failure, corrosive substances and acids, excavation 
hazards, and exposure to hazardous gases, strengthening 
the organisation’s ability to proactively manage high-risk 
operational scenarios. 
Implementation of the CRM framework has significantly 
strengthened safety monitoring and reporting. During the 
year, CRM inspections were conducted across operations 
to ensure the effectiveness of critical controls. Additionally, 
Safety Action Plans (SAPs) were developed during 
FY 2025-26, ensuring systematic closure of identified safety 
gaps. Hazard and Operability Studies (HAZOP) were also 
conducted across all units to identify emerging risks and 
strengthen preventive measures.
To further strengthen leadership capability in safety, we 
conducted S.A.F.E. (Safety Awareness for Excellence in 
Leadership) Workshops for 42 employees, including 33 
Hindustan Zinc employees and 9 business partners. These 
workshops were designed to enhance frontline leadership 
capability, strengthen risk ownership, and reinforce 
behavioural safety practices across operations. Six one-
to-one coaching sessions have been completed for 10 
identified leaders for strengthening leadership accountability 
and enhancing safety culture to drive behavioural change.
We also initiated a Safety Culture Survey pilot at 
Chanderiya Lead-Zinc Smelter, aimed at understanding 
workforce perceptions, identifying improvement areas, 
and strengthening the safety culture across operations. 
Complementing this initiative, focussed Safety Action 
Meetings were conducted with HEMM operators and 
engineering teams to address and prevent hand injuries 
related to HEMM operations.
Business partner engagement remained a key focus area 
during the year. We conducted Business Partner CEO 
Connect sessions, creating a platform to reinforce safety 
accountability, strengthen partnerships, and align business 
partners with Hindustan Zinc's safety standards and 
expectations. We also launched the Mine Safety Assurance 
Programme, aimed at strengthening safety governance 
in mining operations through structured assurance 
mechanisms, periodic reviews, and enhanced oversight of 
risk controls.
The Company continues to invest in strengthening 
infrastructure safety through the Infrastructure Inframatrix 
framework, addressing critical infrastructure risks and 
enhancing operational reliability.
The Company conducted Quantitative Exposure Assessment 
(QNEA), PPE fit assessments and ergonomic studies. As a 
result, 42 high-exposure zones were successfully converted 
into green zones.
