Audit & Risk Management Committee ("ARMC")
The Audit & Risk Management Committee plays a 
central role in the Company’s governance framework by 
providing independent oversight of financial reporting, risk 
management and internal control systems. The Committee 
is responsible for monitoring the integrity of the Company’s 
financial statements, reviewing the effectiveness of risk 
management processes, and overseeing the robustness 
of internal financial controls, including those relating to 
cybersecurity. The Committee also oversees the adequacy 
and effectiveness of the Company’s legal, regulatory 
and ethical compliance framework. In discharging its 
responsibilities, the Committee monitors the qualifications, 
independence, performance and effectiveness of both 
internal and external auditors, and assesses the quality and 
integrity of audit processes on an ongoing basis.
With effect from 06 June 2020, the Audit Committee and 
the Risk Management Committee were consolidated 
into a single Committee, now known as the Audit & Risk 
Management Committee, to enable integrated oversight 
of financial, operational and enterprise‑level risks. The 
management team led by the Executive Director and the 
Head of Management Assurance Services (“MAS”) operates 
as a sub‑structure to the Committee and is responsible 
for implementing and operating the Company’s risk 
management framework. The management periodically 
presents detailed risk assessments and mitigation updates 
to the Committee, including semi‑annual reviews of 
key risks.
Details of the Company’s principal risks and uncertainties, 
along with mitigation strategies, are set out separately in 
the Management Discussion and Analysis section of the 
Integrated Annual Report.
The Committee consists exclusively of Independent 
Directors, ensuring objective and independent judgement 
in matters relating to financial reporting and risk oversight. 
Members of the Committee bring diverse experience and 
strong expertise in finance, accounting, risk management 
and governance. In carrying out its oversight responsibilities, 
the Committee engages closely with management, 
internal auditors and the Statutory Auditors, and may seek 
external expert advice where considered necessary. The 
management remains responsible for the preparation, 
presentation and integrity of the Company’s standalone 
and consolidated financial statements, compliance 
with applicable accounting standards and regulatory 
requirements, and the establishment and maintenance of 
effective internal control systems. M/s S.R. Batliboi & Co. 
LLP, Chartered Accountants (FRN: 301003E/E300005), the 
Statutory Auditors of the Company, conduct an independent 
audit and express an opinion on the true and fair view of the 
financial statements.
The Committee’s agenda covers a broad range of matters, 
including review of quarterly and annual financial results, 
accounting policies and significant judgements, internal 
and external audit observations, related party transactions, 
inter‑corporate loans and investments, and the effectiveness 
of internal control and risk management systems. Through 
these deliberations, the Committee provides assurance 
to the Board on the integrity of financial reporting 
and the adequacy of the Company’s governance and 
control framework.

Mechanism
SEBI has introduced a Common ODR mechanism to 
facilitate online resolution of all kinds of grievances / 
disputes/complaints arising in the Indian Securities 
Market. The said ODR Portal permits the shareholder(s) 
an additional mechanism to resolve the grievances/
complaints/disputes as mentioned below:
Level 1: Approach RTA or the Company
At the initial stage, all grievances/disputes/complaints 
are required to be directly lodged with the RTA/the 
Company. The shareholder(s) may send an email to 
einward.ris@kfintech.com/comp.sect@vedanta.co.in 
or send the physical correspondence addressed to 
M/s. KFin Technologies Limited (Unit: Vedanta Limited), 
Selenium Tower B, Plot No.: 31 & 32, Gachibowli, 
Financial District, Nanakramguda, Serilingampally, 
Hyderabad-500 032, Telangana.
Level 2: Escalate to SEBI SCORES Platform
In case the grievances/disputes/complaints are not 
redressed to the satisfaction of the shareholder(s) at 
Level 1, then the shareholder(s) may escalate the same 
on the SCORES Platform at https://scores.sebi.gov.in/ in 
accordance with the process laid out therein.
Level 3: Initiate Dispute Resolution Process on 
ODR Platform
In case the grievances/disputes/complaints of the 
shareholder(s) are not resolved at Level 1/Level 2, then the 
ODR Process may be initiated through the ODR Portal at 
https://smartodr.in/login within the applicable timeframe 
under law.

The ESG Committee assists the Board in monitoring 
material ESG risks and overseeing the Company’s ESG 
strategy. The Committee meets twice a year and is chaired 
by an Independent Director, and includes participation 
from executive Directors and select KMPs, supporting 
effective alignment between Board oversight and 
management execution.
In FY 2025-26, the Board’s oversight was centered on 
material issues critical to the Company, such as workforce 
safety, decarbonisation and the management of carbon-
related risks, supply chain management, effective oversight 
of tailings facilities, and sustained compliance with 
environmental regulations.
The Board has noted steady progress in the development 
of a comprehensive ESG governance, performance and 
monitoring framework. In line with the Group’s ambition 
of “Transforming for Good”, the Board regularly reviews 
updates on progress across all nine ESG aims, with 
particular focus on the priority areas highlighted above. The 
Board also monitors trends in the Company’s ESG ratings, 
recognising that assessments by agencies such as MSCI, 
Sustainalytics and S&P have a bearing on the Group’s 
reputation and access to capital. In this context, the Board 
has acknowledged the Group’s efforts in establishing and 
strengthening VEDAS, a digital‑first sustainability training 
platform aimed at achieving 100% employee coverage over 
a three‑year period.
While the Board‑level ESG Committee has taken note of the 
reduction in fatal incidents across the Group’s operations, 
ensuring safe and healthy working conditions continues to 
remain a key priority. The Committee seeks regular updates 
on the implementation of learnings from past incidents, 
outcomes of assessments conducted under the Critical Risk 
Management programme, and progress on infrastructure 
and system‑led improvements to prevent workplace injuries.

are provided in earlier section of the Corporate 
Governance Report.

Commodity Price Risk or Foreign Exchange Risk 
and Hedging Activities
Fluctuation in commodity prices
Impact: Prices and demand for the Group’s products 
are expected to remain volatile/uncertain and strongly 
influenced by global economic conditions. Volatility in 
commodity prices and demand may adversely affect our 
earnings, cash flow and reserves.
Mitigation: Our Group has a well-diversified portfolio, which 
acts as a hedge against fluctuations in commodities and 
delivers cash flows through the cycle. We consider exposure 
to commodity price fluctuations to be an integral part of our 
Group’s business and its usual policy is to sell its products 
at prevailing market prices, and not to enter into long-term 
price hedging arrangements. However, to minimise price 
risk for finished goods where price of raw material is also 
determined by same underlying base metal prices (e.g. 
purchase of alumina, copper concentrate for manufacturing 
and selling copper and aluminium products, respectively) we 
employ back-to-back hedging. In exceptional circumstances, 
we may enter into strategic hedging with prior approval of 
the EXCO. The Group monitors the commodity markets 
closely to determine the effect of price fluctuations on 
earnings, capital expenditure and cash flows.
Currency exchange rate fluctuations
Impact: Our assets, earnings and cash flows are influenced 
by a variety of currencies due to the diversity of the countries 
in which we operate. Fluctuations in exchange rates of those 
currencies may have an impact on our financials. Although 
the majority of the Group’s revenue is tied to commodity 
prices that are typically priced by reference to the US dollar, 
a significant part of its expenses are incurred and paid in 
local currency. Moreover, some of the Group borrowings 
are denominated in US dollars, while a large percentage of 
cash and liquid investments are held in other currencies, 
mainly in the Indian rupee. Any material fluctuations of 
these currencies against the US dollar could result in 
lower profitability or in higher cash outflows towards 
debt obligations.
Mitigation: We do not speculate in forex. We have developed 
robust controls in forex management to monitor, measure 
and hedge currency risk liabilities. The Committee of 
Directors reviews our forex-related matters periodically and 
suggests necessary courses of action as may be needed 
by businesses from time to time, and within the overall 
framework of our forex policy.
Exposures on foreign currency loans are managed 
through the Group wide hedging policy, which is reviewed 
periodically to ensure that the results from fluctuating 
currency exchange rates are appropriately managed. The 
Group strives to achieve asset liability offset of foreign 
currency exposures and only the net position is hedged. The 
Group uses forward exchange contracts, currency swaps 
and other derivatives to hedge the effects of movements 
in exchange rates on foreign currency denominated assets 
and liabilities. The sources of foreign exchange risk are 
outstanding amounts payable for imported raw materials, 
capital goods and other supplies as well as financing 
transactions and loans denominated in foreign currencies. 
The Group is also exposed to foreign exchange risk on 
its net investment in foreign operations. Most of these 
transactions are denominated in US dollars. Short-term net 
exposures are hedged progressively based on their maturity. 
A more conservative approach has been adopted for project 
expenditures to avoid budget overruns, where cost of the 
project is calculated taking into account the hedge cost. 
However, all new long-term borrowing exposures are being 
hedged. The hedge mechanisms are reviewed periodically 
to ensure that the risk from fluctuating currency exchange 
rates is appropriately managed.

The Board of Vedanta Limited has constituted key committees to oversee sustainability, governance, 
and compliance, ensuring alignment with its strategic priorities. The principal committees include:
ESG Committee: The Board-level ESG Committee oversees all sustainability and ESG matters. It works 
closely with the Corporate Sustainability and ESG function to drive and monitor initiatives under the 
Transforming for Good agenda. The Committee is appointed by the Board, chaired by a Non-Executive 
Director, and includes at least one Independent Director. The Group HSE & Sustainability Head and ESG 
Director are permanent invitees.
Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Committee: The CSR Committee supervises the Company’s 
CSR initiatives, recommends the annual CSR plan and resource allocation to the Board, and reviews 
performance against approved plans.
Audit and Risk Management Committee: This Committee oversees financial reporting, internal controls, 
and risk management frameworks, including cybersecurity. It monitors strategic, operational, financial, 
sustainability, and compliance risks, and evaluates the performance and independence of auditors.
Stakeholders’ Relationship Committee (SRC): The SRC focusses on stakeholder engagement, ensuring 
timely resolution of shareholder grievances, improving shareholder experience, and overseeing registrar 
and shareholding-related matters.
For additional information on the roles and responsibilities of the above-mentioned Committees and 
their members, please refer to the Corporate Governance section on page 322 of the Integrated Annual 
Report FY 2025–26.

3.	
Describe the processes in place to safely reclaim your products for reusing, recycling, and disposing at the end of 
life, for (a) plastic (including packing) (b) e-waste (c) hazardous waste and (d) other waste.
	
This indicator is not applicable to Vedanta Limited, as our business primarily operates on a B2B model, supplying our 
products as raw materials to various industries. However, Vedanta’s waste management philosophy is rooted in its 
Waste-to-Wealth commitment. While end of life product reclamation is not relevant to our core operations, circular 
economy principles are deeply embedded across our value chain, focussing on minimising waste disposal, maximising 
resource efficiency, and converting process residues into value added materials.
	
Governance Framework
	
All business units are governed by Vedanta’s Technical Standard on Resource Use and Waste Management, aligned 
with the Basel Convention, ICMM Principles, and IFC Performance Standards. Waste management is structured around 
the hierarchy:
	
Avoid  Reduce  Reuse  Recycle  Recover  Treat  Dispose
	
Compliance is mandated under the Hazardous Waste Rules 2016, E-Waste Management Rules, Plastic Waste 
Management Rules, and applicable State Pollution Control Board (SPCB) requirements. Vedanta’s long-term ambition is 
to achieve Zero Waste to Landfill across all operations.
	
Plastic Waste
	
Bulk dispatch of metals and minerals means plastic packaging is minimal. Where plastic waste arises, it is segregated at 
source and channelled through authorised recyclers. Notably:
	•
HZL, BALCO, and TSPL operate under a strict single-use plastic prohibition
	•
TSPL and Cairn hold CII Single-Use Plastic-Free certification
	•
Meenakshi Energy maintains a traceable scrap yard management system
	
E-Waste
	
Not a material stream for core operations. All e-waste from IT, instrumentation, and administrative equipment 
is disposed of exclusively through government authorised recyclers, with full inventory tracking and recycling 
certification maintained.
	
Hazardous Waste
	
Classified and managed under the Basel Convention and Hazardous Waste Rules 2016. Key streams such as spent oils, 
refractories, spent pot lining, smelter residues are managed through a recovery-first approach:
	•
Co-processing in cement kilns as an alternative fuel
	•
Treatment through registered recyclers
	•
Disposal at authorised TSDFs only, via SPCB approved vendors
	•
Used oil re-refined through certified agencies
	
Robust manifest systems ensure end to end traceability and regulatory compliance.
	
High-Volume, Low-Toxicity (HVLT) Waste and Other Non-Hazardous Waste
	
HVLT streams: ash, red mud, jarofix, slag, and lime grit are inherent to metals and mining operations. All are stored 
in scientifically engineered facilities, including tailings dams and ash dykes, under continuous geotechnical and 
environmental monitoring.
	
Circular utilisation is prioritised over disposal. Fly ash is supplied to the cement and construction industries; slag is 
channelled into road construction and building materials; jarofix serves as structural fill. Red mud valorisation initiatives 
are currently under development. Remaining non-hazardous waste is managed through recycling, composting, and, as a 
last resort, scientifically managed landfill.

Yes, Extended Producer Responsibility (EPR) applies to specific business units of Vedanta Limited where regulatory

channelled to authorised recyclers, including co-processing in cement plants where appropriate.
	
Furthermore, all business units ensure that plastic packaging materials received, particularly for imported goods, are 
segregated at the source and routed for recycling through authorised agencies, in line with approved EPR action plans.

10.	 Health and safety management system:
	
a. 	
Whether an occupational health and safety management system has been implemented by the entity? (Yes/ No). 
If yes, the coverage of such a system?
	
	
Yes, Vedanta has established a comprehensive Occupational Health and Safety Management System aligned 
with International Council on Mining and Metals (ICMM) guidelines, International Finance Corporation (IFC) 
recommendations, and applicable global standards. The framework is implemented across all operations, 
including subsidiaries, joint ventures, associates, and acquisitions, ensuring a consistent and rigorous approach to 
workplace safety.
	
	
The company is committed to achieving excellence in health and safety management, with a strong focus on 
eliminating unsafe conditions and practices. Its operations are certified to ISO 45001:2018, reflecting adherence to 
internationally recognised standards.
	
	
Governance is reinforced through a robust oversight structure, supported by the Vedanta Safety Performance 
Standard, which enables systematic monitoring and continuous improvement across all business units.
	
b.	
What are the processes used to identify work-related hazards and assess risks on a routine and non-routine 
basis by the entity?
	
	
Vedanta adopts a structured and multi-layered approach to identify and manage work-related hazards across 
routine and non-routine activities, aligned with ISO 45001:2018 and internal risk assessment standards.
	
	
Routine Risk Identification and Control
	•
Hazard Identification and Risk Assessment (HIRA) and Job Safety Analysis (JSA) are used to identify task-level 
risks and implement preventive controls.
	•
Standard Operating Procedures are developed and periodically updated to ensure safe and consistent practices.
	•
Site-level HIRA registers are maintained and regularly updated to reflect operational changes and emerging risks.
	
	
Advanced Risk Assessment for Non-Routine Activities
	•
Hazard Identification Study (HAZID), Hazard and Operability Study (HAZOP), and Quantitative Risk Assessment 
(QRA) are used for complex and high-risk scenarios.
	•
A Permit-to-Work (PTW) system ensures that such activities proceed only after thorough risk assessment and 
control implementation.
	•
Simultaneous Operations (SIMOPS) reviews are conducted to manage overlapping risks.
	
	
Critical Risk Management (CRM)
	•
A structured CRM programme identifies and manages critical risks across operations based on 
ICMM methodology.
	•
Key risks include working at height, energy release, confined spaces, electrical hazards, loss of containment, 
vehicle pedestrian interaction, uncontrolled loads during lifting, uncontrolled release of energy, and loss of 
containment of molten material.
	•
Controls are continuously strengthened based on incident data and risk evaluations.
	
	
Workforce Engagement and Monitoring
	•
Toolbox Talks (TBTs) are conducted regularly to communicate task-specific risks and reinforce safe practices at 
the worksite.
	•
Safety interactions, Visible Felt Leadership visits, and Contractor Safety Field Audits support ongoing monitoring 
and compliance.
	•
A digital platform (Enablon) enables data-driven tracking, assessments, and corrective actions.
	
	
This integrated framework ensures proactive risk identification, effective mitigation, and continuous improvement, 
supporting Vedanta’s commitment to a zero-harm workplace.
	
c. 	
Whether you have processes for workers to report the work-related hazards and to remove themselves from 
such risks. (Y/N)
	
	
Yes, Ensuring a safe and responsive work environment, Vedanta has put in place robust systems that enable 
workers to report hazards and step away from unsafe conditions when required. The Company’s digital platform, 
“V-Unified”, provides a centralised channel for employees, workers, and visitors to log safety concerns, facilitating 
effective tracking, timely intervention, and closure. In parallel, site-level healthiness scores are continuously 
monitored to strengthen safety controls and drive improvements in workplace conditions.
	
	
Proactive hazard identification is reinforced through structured safety practices such as regular safety interactions, 
planned hazard tours, and critical risk verification exercises across operations. These efforts are further supported 
by AI-enabled monitoring tools, including T-Pulse cameras, which help identify and flag unsafe acts and conditions 
in real time.

12.	 Describe the measures taken by the entity to ensure a safe and healthy workplace.
	
Vedanta has established a Group-wide Health, Safety and Environment (HSE) framework comprising technical standards, 
management systems and site-specific safety programmes, with “zero harm” as the overarching objective. 
	
Critical Risk Management and Infrastructure
	
The Critical Risk Management (CRM) programme identifies 17 critical risks based on historical incident data. Control 
measures have been defined for each risk and are subject to continuous monitoring at the shop-floor level by line 
functions. The Infra-Matrix framework is deployed across sites to map critical risks with corresponding physical safety 
infrastructure, including pedestrian pathways, man-machine segregation corridors, conveyor guarding and restricted-
access zones.
	
Engineering Controls
	
The Company undertook targeted interventions to eliminate or mitigate risks at source. Key initiatives include:
•	 BALCO: 21 km of a 23-km man-machine segregation corridor commissioned; 2 km in progress
	•
VAL–Lanjigarh: Wagon tippler installed for bauxite unloading, eliminating manual worker exposure to wagon door 
line-of-fire
	•
ESL Steel: Segregation of routes for raw material vehicles and personal vehicles to avoid interaction between heavy 
vehicle and personal vehicles
	•
Athena Power: Integration of Enablon for health risk tracking to conduct risk identification and closure proactively
	•
MEL Nickel: Installation of Isolators to eliminate the need of isolation inside the group feeders to avoid direct touch of 
panel when in live
	
Behavior-Based Safety and Culture
	
Behavior-based safety programmes, including Visible Felt Leadership (VFL), CRM audits and Contractor Field Safety 
Audits, are implemented across sites to identify and address unsafe acts and conditions. Cairn Oil & Gas continues 
to operate a structured observation programme to maintain LTIFR and TRIFR within defined targets. ESL Steel is 
implementing a safety culture transformation programme (‘Prarambhik’) with external advisory support, with progressive 
ownership by line functions. AI-enabled surveillance systems have been deployed at Silvassa for real-time monitoring of 
unsafe behaviours.
	
Training and Emergency Preparedness
	
Mandatory safety induction is conducted for all personnel prior to site entry. Regular Toolbox Talks, Pre-Activity Briefings 
(PAP Talks) and Pre-Job Safety Meetings are conducted across shifts. Competency-based training is ensured prior 
to authorisation for hazardous operations. Emergency preparedness is strengthened through periodic mock drills 
conducted across locations, including ESL Steel and Fujairah. At Fujairah, remote working protocols and contingency 
plans were activated in response to regional developments.
	
Occupational Health
	
Pre-employment and periodic medical examinations are conducted for all employees and contract workers, as 
applicable. Long-term health surveillance programmes are in place at select units, supported by engineering controls for 
ventilation, dust and noise management. Chemical safety measures, including installation of Diphoterine stations, and 
occupational health risk assessments have been implemented at MEL Nickel.
	
Safety Governance
	
A Group-level, CEO sponsored committee oversees CRM implementation, safety infrastructure and injury prevention 
initiatives. Safety alerts issued post any fatal incident are tracked for closure of corrective and preventive actions across 
all business units to enable cross-functional learning and strengthen accountability.
	
Through these measures, Vedanta continues to build a culture where safety is non-negotiable, embedding accountability 
at every level of the organisation, from the shop floor to the boardroom, and driving measurable progress towards a zero-
harm workplace across all its operations and geographies.

1.	
Provide the processes for consultation between stakeholders and the Board on economic, environmental, and social 
topics or if consultation is delegated, how is feedback from such consultations provided to the Board
	
Vedanta follows a structured and multi-tiered approach to stakeholder consultation, ensuring that insights on economic, 
environmental, and social matters are effectively captured and escalated to the Board. Stakeholder engagement is an 
ongoing process, led by business and functional leadership through formal engagement platforms across all operations. 
Each business unit implements a defined stakeholder engagement plan, with unit heads responsible for conducting 
regular interactions and capturing stakeholder feedback.
	
Inputs gathered from these engagements are periodically reviewed at the business unit level and form the basis for 
further consultations with senior management, including the CEO. Key outcomes and strategic insights from such 
interactions are subsequently presented to the Board during quarterly meetings, enabling informed decision-making at 
the highest level.
	
Community-related feedback is systematically reviewed through Social Performance Committee meetings at the unit 
level and further deliberated at the Corporate Social Responsibility (CSR) Committee. In addition, independent third-party 
assessments including baseline studies, impact assessments, and need assessments conducted at periodic intervals 
provide structured feedback from stakeholders, which is presented to the CSR Committee of the Board.
	
At the governance level, the Board ESG and Sustainability Committee oversees stakeholder-related matters, including 
periodic review of stakeholder groups and their material concerns. Stakeholder inputs are also integrated into the 
Company’s materiality assessment process, which is reassessed in consultation with stakeholders.
	
Furthermore, shareholders are provided with a formal platform to engage directly with the Board during the Annual 
General Meeting (AGM), ensuring transparency and accountability. Through this integrated framework, Vedanta 
ensures that stakeholder perspectives are systematically incorporated into Board-level deliberations and strategic 
decision making.
2.	
Whether stakeholder consultation is used to support the identification and management of environmental and social 
topics (Yes / No). If so, provide details of instances as to how the inputs received from stakeholders on these topics 
were incorporated into policies and activities of the entity
	
Yes, Stakeholder consultation is integral to Vedanta’s identification, prioritisation and management of environmental and 
social topics, and forms the basis of its materiality assessment process.
	
In FY 2024–25, the Company conducted a Group-wide double materiality assessment, engaging internal and external 
stakeholders through structured tools and consultations. Stakeholders included communities, regulators, investors, 
employees and civil society organisations. Inputs were assessed across impact and financial materiality, and prioritised 
based on severity and likelihood in line with ICMM requirements. The outcomes informed Vedanta’s KPIs, policies and 
sustainability programmes.
	
In FY 2025–26, stakeholder engagement continues through ongoing interactions across community, investor, regulatory 
and employee channels, enabling timely identification of emerging issues and alignment of ESG priorities with 
stakeholder expectations.
3.	
Provide details of instances of engagement with, and actions taken to, address the concerns of vulnerable/ 
marginalised stakeholder groups
	
Vedanta adopts an inclusive and participatory approach to engaging with vulnerable and marginalised stakeholder 
groups, with programmes designed to address their evolving needs and improve socio-economic outcomes. These 
initiatives are informed by ongoing community interactions, baseline assessments, and feedback mechanisms to ensure 
relevance and effectiveness. Key interventions include:
	•
Women Empowerment: Through programmes such as Sakhi and women’s self-help groups, Vedanta supports 
capacity building, access to finance, and enterprise development, enabling women to enhance their livelihoods and 
participate more actively in community decision-making.
	•
Child Development and Education: The Nand Ghar initiative, implemented in collaboration with the Ministry of Women 
and Child Development, focusses on transforming anganwadis into modern centres that provide integrated services, 
including nutrition, early learning, and healthcare support for children and mothers.
	•
Healthcare Outreach: Vedanta strengthens access to healthcare in remote and underserved areas through mobile 
health units, medical camps, support to primary health centres, and availability of specialised medical services, 
addressing critical health gaps within communities.
	•
Livelihood Promotion: Targeted livelihood programmes in agriculture, allied activities, and micro-enterprises are 
implemented to enhance income opportunities for marginalised groups, with a particular focus on rural households 
and women-led initiatives.
	•
Community Engagement: A structured engagement process enables continuous dialogue with communities, 
facilitating identification of concerns, co-creation of solutions, and effective grievance resolution, ensuring that 
marginalised voices are actively considered in decision-making.
Through these focussed efforts, Vedanta continues to promote inclusive growth and strengthen the resilience of vulnerable 
communities across its areas of operation.

Do you have a focal point (Individual/ Committee) responsible for addressing human rights impacts or issues caused 
or contributed to by the business? (Yes/No)
	
Yes, Vedanta has a defined governance structure with designated focal points at both Group and operational levels 
responsible for identifying, managing, and addressing human rights impacts.
	
At the Group level, the Board ESG Committee provides oversight of Vedanta’s Human Rights Policy, approved by the 
Board, reviewing it annually and recommending updates. The Executive Sustainability Committee, chaired by the CEO 
and comprising senior leaders, oversees the identification and management of social and human rights risks across 
project lifecycles.
	
At the operational level, Social Performance Steering Committees (SPSCs) are established at all sites, adopting a 
cross-functional approach that draws on External Affairs, Operations, Security, CSR, HR, HSE, Finance, and Corporate 
Communications. Each function carries defined responsibilities for preventing and addressing specific human rights 
concerns, covering wages, working hours, child and forced labour, health and safety, discrimination, and freedom 
of association. The Social Performance Manager convenes the SPSC, supported by a Community Liaison Officer 
responsible for regular community interactions and timely grievance resolution.
	
Every operational unit additionally maintains a Grievance Redressal Committee with a structured grievance-
handling procedure, accessible through formal reporting systems, grievance boxes at prominent site locations, and 
confidential whistleblowing channels. An Internal Complaints Committee handles human rights grievances requiring 
formal adjudication.
	
Human rights awareness training is provided to employees and security personnel, reinforcing the governance structure 
with competency at the ground level.
5.	
Describe the internal mechanisms in place to redress grievances related to human rights issues.
	
Aligned with the Vedanta Sustainability Framework (VSF), the grievance mechanism is designed to be accessible, 
confidential, culturally appropriate, and free of cost and retaliation for all complainants, including employees, workers, 
contractors, and community members.
	
Channels for Submission
	
Grievances can be raised verbally or in writing through face-to-face meetings, phone calls, letters, dedicated email 
addresses, physical grievance boxes at site locations, and confidential whistleblowing channels.
	
Tiered Resolution Structure
	•
First Order: Direct resolution between the Company and complainant, with formal acknowledgement within two 
business days and progress updates every 15 days
	•
Second Order: Unresolved complaints are referred to an independent third party for mediation
	•
Third Order: Matters not resolved through the above are escalated to judicial processes
	
Oversight and Tracking
	
A Grievance Response Committee, comprising the General Manager (or delegate), Social Performance Manager, and 
relevant department heads, oversees investigations, corrective actions, and closure. All grievances are registered, 
tracked, and analysed in a secure system to identify patterns and ensure timely resolution. Target resolution is within 30 
days; where this is not achievable, the Community Liaison Officer updates both the Social Performance Manager and the 
grievance holder on a bimonthly basis.
	
Post-resolution, feedback is obtained from the grievance holder on the redressal experience. The Social Performance 
Manager monitors quarterly performance of the mechanism against defined outcome indicators, sharing findings with 
the location head, SPSC, and Corporate HSES.
	
pecialised committees, including Internal Complaints Committees (ICCs) for sexual harassment and related matters, 
operate in parallel, ensuring compliance with applicable legal requirements and providing safe, dedicated channels for 
specific categories of concern.
	
This mechanism aligns with the UN Guiding Principles on Business and Human Rights, reinforcing Vedanta’s 
commitment to dignified, fair, and effective redressal across all operations.

8.	
Mechanism to prevent adverse consequences to the complainant in discrimination and harassment cases.
	
The Company is committed to fostering a safe, equitable, and inclusive workplace, underpinned by a zero-tolerance 
approach to discrimination and harassment. This commitment is operationalised through its Diversity & Inclusion 
Policy, Human Rights Policy, and Policy on Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal of Sexual Harassment, aligned with the 
provisions of the Sexual Harassment of Women at Workplace (Prevention, Prohibition and Redressal) Act, 2013.
	
To safeguard complainants against any adverse consequences, the Company has instituted robust and structured 
mechanisms, including:
	•
Confidentiality and Protection Measures: All complaints are handled with strict confidentiality to protect the identity 
and privacy of the complainant. Appropriate interim relief measures—such as change in reporting structure, transfer 
of workplace, or grant of leave—are provided, where necessary, to ensure safety and prevent any form of retaliation.
	•
Non-Retaliation Commitment: The Company enforces a strong non-retaliation framework through its Human Rights 
and POSH policies, explicitly prohibiting any form of victimisation or adverse action against individuals who raise 
concerns in good faith.
	•
Institutional Mechanism (ICC): An Internal Complaints Committee (ICC), constituted in compliance with 
statutory requirements, is responsible for the fair, impartial, and time-bound investigation of complaints related to 
sexual harassment.
	•
Fair and Independent Investigation: A structured investigation process is followed to assess the merits of each 
complaint, ensuring due process, neutrality, and sensitivity. This includes gathering evidence, examining witnesses, 
and maintaining procedural integrity.
	•
Remedial and Disciplinary Actions: Where allegations are substantiated, the Company undertakes appropriate 
corrective actions, including disciplinary measures against the respondent, policy revisions, and targeted training 
interventions to prevent recurrence.
	•
Grievance Redressal and Support Systems: In addition to the ICC, a formal grievance redressal mechanism is in 
place to address broader concerns related to discrimination and workplace conduct. Complainants are also provided 
access to counselling and support services to address emotional and psychological well-being.
	
Through these integrated measures, Vedanta ensures that individuals can report concerns without fear, thereby 
reinforcing a culture of trust, accountability, and respect across the organisation.

Yes, Vedanta Limited has implemented Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) mechanisms across multiple operations, particularly 
at facilities located in water-stressed regions. The Company remains committed to responsible water stewardship by 
ensuring that treated wastewater is fully recycled within plant boundaries, and no process effluent is discharged outside 
operational premises.
	
ZLD systems are implemented at the following business units: Hindustan Zinc Limited (HZL), BALCO, TSPL, Athena 
Power, ESL Steel Limited, IOK, Vazare, Jamkhani Coal Mines, Vedanta Aluminium (Jharsuguda and Lanjigarh), Silvassa, 
Fujairah, MEL Nickel, Black Mountain, Gamsberg Operations and VGCB.
	
Implementation Framework
	
Across the units, ZLD is achieved through a combination of:
	•
Effluent Treatment Plants (ETPs) and Sewage Treatment Plants (STPs) for treating industrial and 
domestic wastewater
	•
Advanced wastewater treatment technologies, including filtration, reverse osmosis and evaporation systems
	•
Recycling and reuse of treated water for process applications, cooling tower makeup, ash handling, dust suppression 
and horticulture
	•
Engineered storage systems to prevent groundwater contamination
	•
Real-time monitoring systems including flow meters, piezometers and Pan-Tilt-Zoom (PTZ) cameras
	•
Continuous online effluent monitoring systems with live data connectivity to the Central Pollution Control Board 
(CPCB), wherever applicable
	
In aluminium operations, wastewater from bauxite residue management is fully recovered and reused, and the residue is 
safely stored in scientifically engineered and monitored facilities. The thermal power unit (TSPL) operates under ZLD by 
treating coaly wastewater, oily wastewater, industrial effluent, and cooling tower blowdown for complete internal reuse.
	
Through these measures, Vedanta ensures compliance with regulatory standards while significantly reducing freshwater 
dependency and strengthening water circularity across operations.

10.	 Briefly describe the waste management practices adopted in your establishments. Describe the strategy adopted by 
your company to reduce usage of hazardous and toxic chemicals in your products and processes and the practices 
adopted to manage such wastes.
	
Vedanta Limited implements an integrated waste management framework designed to minimise environmental 
impact through source reduction, resource recovery, and responsible disposal. The Company adopts a lifecycle-based 
approach to waste, with a strong emphasis on maximising by-product utilisation, including 100% utilisation of ash, 
while progressively eliminating legacy waste by 2035 and legacy ash by 2030. Hazardous waste streams are governed 
by stringent operational controls, independently audited tailings management systems, and real-time monitoring 
mechanisms to ensure environmental integrity and regulatory compliance.
	
In parallel, Vedanta systematically reduces the use of hazardous and toxic chemicals by deploying cleaner production 
technologies, optimising process efficiency, and substituting high-risk substances with safer alternatives wherever 
feasible. Anchored in its “Zero Harm, Zero Waste, Zero Discharge” philosophy, the Company prioritises prevention at 
source, material recovery, recycling, and safe treatment to mitigate environmental and health risks across its operations.
	
Beyond routine compliance and waste handling practices, Vedanta has implemented the following advanced initiatives to 
strengthen circularity, reduce hazardous waste generation, and enhance sustainable resource utilisation:
	
Circular Economy & Resource Recovery
	
– Achieved 101% ash utilisation in FY 2025-26 through structured monitoring and end-use partnerships.
	
– Commissioned a Fumer plant, eliminating jarosite generation at one Hydro Zinc Smelter; resultant slag is fully utilised 
in cement manufacturing.
	
– Commissioned a residue treatment plant at Chanderiya Lead-Zinc Smelter to enhance metal recovery from process 
waste.
	
– Implemented sodium sulphate recovery from RO reject at Dariba Zinc Smelter.
	
– Utilised jarosite, jarofix, slag, fly ash, and tailings in cement manufacturing, road construction, and underground mine 
backfilling (paste fill/hydrofill).
	
Water Stewardship & Zero Liquid Discharge
	
– Maintained Zero Liquid Discharge (ZLD) across most operations.
	
– Recycled approximately 90 million kL of water in FY 2025-26, reducing freshwater withdrawal and preventing water 
pollution.
	
Tailings & Hazardous Waste Management
	
– Operated 16 active tailings facilities, all independently audited.
	
– Deployed dry tailings disposal technology at select sites to reduce long-term environmental risk.
	
– Established secure storage infrastructure for used oil, lead-acid batteries, and fluoride-bearing hazardous waste 
(Jharsuguda).
	
– Commissioned a hazardous waste incinerator with a double scrubbing system.
	
– Disposed of hazardous waste through authorised recyclers and TSDF facilities; non-hazardous waste managed 
through structured scrap recovery systems.
	
Reduction of Hazardous & Toxic Chemicals
	
– Implemented risk-based chemical prioritisation and lifecycle monitoring (Cairn Ravva site).
	
– Engaged suppliers to identify and adopt greener substitutes.
	
– Applied green chemistry principles and continuous process optimisation.
	
– Conducted employee training and ensured strict regulatory compliance.
	
Innovation & Strategic Partnerships
	
– Developed a breakthrough process to recover battery-grade graphite from Spent Pot Lining (SPL) and Shot Blast Dust 
(Vedanta Aluminium).
	
– Produced biomass briquettes from agricultural residues, supporting circular economy objectives.
	
– Partnered with VEXL Environ Projects to convert jarosite and jarofix into usable resources (Hindustan Zinc Ltd.).

3.	
With respect to the ecologically sensitive areas reported at Question 11 of Essential Indicators above, provide 
details of significant direct & indirect impact of the entity on biodiversity in such areas along-with prevention and 
remediation activities
	
Vedanta adopts a proactive and science-based approach to managing biodiversity impacts in ecologically sensitive 
areas. The Company conducts comprehensive assessments of both direct and indirect impacts across the entire 
operational lifecycle — from exploration and project planning to operation and closure — and implements robust 
prevention, mitigation, and remediation measures aligned with sustainable development principles.
	
Significant Direct and Indirect Impacts on Biodiversity
	
Direct Impacts
	
Direct impacts primarily arise from operational and infrastructure activities, including:
	•
Habitat loss and fragmentation resulting from infrastructure development such as tailings dams, water reservoirs, 
processing plants, and access roads
	•
Air emissions and effluent discharge affecting terrestrial and aquatic ecosystems
	•
Disturbance from exploration drilling and mining operations
	•
Introduction of invasive alien species, whether accidental or intentional, potentially disrupting native ecosystems
	
Indirect Impacts
	
Indirect impacts extend beyond immediate operations and may include:
	•
Supply chain-related biodiversity impacts, such as the production and transportation of materials and equipment
	•
Ecosystem alterations due to pollution, including chemical discharges and water contamination
	•
Noise pollution and habitat disturbance, influencing wildlife movement and behaviour
	•
Climate change impacts associated with greenhouse gas emissions from fossil fuel extraction and processing
	
Prevention, Mitigation and Remediation Measures
	
Vedanta implements a structured mitigation framework guided by the mitigation hierarchy — Avoid, Minimise, Restore, 
Offset — to ensure responsible biodiversity stewardship.
	•
Biodiversity Risk Assessment and Management: Conducting baseline surveys and ecological risk screenings to 
identify sensitive areas and integrate mitigation measures into project planning.
	•
Biodiversity Management Plans (BMPs): Developing site-specific plans outlining prevention, mitigation, restoration, 
conservation actions, and ongoing monitoring.
	•
No Net Loss (NNL) and Net Positive Impact (NPI): Targeting no net loss of biodiversity and striving for net positive 
impact in critical habitats through on-site and off-site conservation and restoration initiatives.
	•
Habitat Restoration and Conservation: Implementing reforestation with native and fruit-bearing species, groundwater 
recharge through water reservoirs, and wildlife-support initiatives such as butterfly parks, birdhouses, and 
artificial nests.
	•
Invasive Species Control: Conducting pre-introduction risk assessments and implementing monitoring and eradication 
measures to prevent and manage invasive alien species.
	•
Community and Employee Engagement: Promoting biodiversity stewardship through awareness programmes, water 
body clean-up initiatives, and capacity-building activities.
	•
Compliance and Strategic Integration: Ensuring compliance with local, national, and international biodiversity 
standards, while embedding biodiversity considerations into strategic planning, financial decisions, and 
lifecycle management.
	
Through this comprehensive framework, Vedanta seeks to responsibly manage biodiversity risks, enhance ecosystem 
resilience, and contribute meaningfully to long-term environmental sustainability.

Describe the mechanisms to receive and redress grievances of the community
	
Yes, Vedanta has a structured community grievance redressal mechanism embedded within its Vedanta Sustainability 
Framework (VSF), designed to be accessible, transparent, and resolution focussed at the site level.
	
Channels for Submission
	
Grievances are received through Community Liaison Officers (CLOs), grievance boxes placed outside plant gates, and 
written submissions in local languages — ensuring accessibility for all community members.
	
Seven-Step Resolution Process
	
All grievances follow a defined sequence: Receive  Acknowledge  Assess & Assign  Investigate  Respond  
Resolve/Recourse  Close-out. Acknowledgement is provided within 24 hours (maximum two business days), with 
progress updates every 30 days.
	
Tiered Escalation Structure
	•
First Order: Direct resolution between the Company and complainant at site level
	•
Second Order: Unresolved grievances escalated to a third-party mediator with complainant consent
	•
Third Order: Legal recourse as a last resort, initiated by either party
	
Site-Level Governance
	
Each location has a Social Performance Steering Committee (SPSC), chaired by the Social Performance Manager, 
overseeing grievance discussion and timely closure. At HZL, resolution is targeted within 15 days with escalation to 
senior management if unresolved. At TSPL, the CLO ensures resolution within 30 days, with bimonthly updates provided 
for pending cases. At VAL–Jharsuguda, a Grievance Response Committee comprising the CLO, SP Manager, and General 
Manager determines the Company’s response within five days of investigation findings, communicating resolutions both 
verbally and in writing.
	
All business units maintain detailed grievance records to identify patterns, assess training needs, and continuously 
improve community engagement practices.

Report on the Internal Financial Controls under 
Clause (i) of Sub-section 3 of Section 143 of the 
Companies Act, 2013 (“the Act”)
In conjunction with our audit of the consolidated financial 
statements of Vedanta Limited (hereinafter referred to as 
the “Holding Company”) as of and for the year ended March 
31, 2026, we have audited the internal financial controls 
with reference to consolidated financial statements of the 
Holding Company and its subsidiaries (the Holding Company 
and its subsidiaries together referred to as “the Group”), its 
associates, joint ventures and joint operation, which are 
companies incorporated in India, as of that date.
Management’s Responsibility for Internal 
Financial Controls
The respective Board of Directors of the companies 
included in the Group, its associates, joint ventures and 
joint operation, which are companies incorporated in India, 
are responsible for establishing and maintaining internal 
financial controls based on the internal control over financial 
reporting criteria established by the Holding Company 
considering the essential components of internal control 
stated in the Guidance Note on Audit of Internal Financial 
Controls Over Financial Reporting issued by the Institute of 
Chartered Accountants of India (ICAI). These responsibilities 
include the design, implementation and maintenance of 
adequate internal financial controls that were operating 
effectively for ensuring the orderly and efficient conduct 
of its business, including adherence to the respective 
company’s policies, the safeguarding of its assets, the 
prevention and detection of frauds and errors, the accuracy 
and completeness of the accounting records, and the timely 
preparation of reliable financial information, as required 
under the Companies Act, 2013.
Auditor’s Responsibility
Our responsibility is to express an opinion on the Holding 
Company’s internal financial controls with reference to 
consolidated financial statements based on our audit. 
We conducted our audit in accordance with the Guidance 
Note on Audit of Internal Financial Controls Over Financial 
Reporting (the “Guidance Note”) and the Standards on 
Auditing, specified under section 143(10) of the Act, to the 
extent applicable to an audit of internal financial controls, 
both, issued by ICAI. Those Standards and the Guidance 
Note require that we comply with ethical requirements and 
plan and perform the audit to obtain reasonable assurance 
about whether adequate internal financial controls with 
reference to consolidated financial statements was 
established and maintained and if such controls operated 
effectively in all material respects.
Annexure 2 
To the Independent Auditor’s Report of even date on the Consolidated Financial Statements of Vedanta Limited
Our audit involves performing procedures to obtain audit 
evidence about the adequacy of the internal financial 
controls with reference to consolidated financial statements 
and their operating effectiveness. Our audit of internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements included obtaining an understanding of internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements, assessing the risk that a material weakness 
exists, and testing and evaluating the design and operating 
effectiveness of internal control based on the assessed 
risk. The procedures selected depend on the auditor’s 
judgement, including the assessment of the risks of material 
misstatement of the financial statements, whether due to 
fraud or error.
We believe that the audit evidence we have obtained and 
the audit evidence obtained by the other auditors in terms 
of their reports referred to in the Other Matters paragraph 
below, is sufficient and appropriate to provide a basis for our 
audit opinion on the internal financial controls with reference 
to consolidated financial statements.
Meaning of Internal Financial Controls With 
Reference to Consolidated Financial Statements
A company’s internal financial control with reference to 
consolidated financial statements is a process designed 
to provide reasonable assurance regarding the reliability 
of financial reporting and the preparation of financial 
statements for external purposes in accordance with 
generally accepted accounting principles. A company’s 
internal financial control with reference to consolidated 
financial statements includes those policies and 
procedures that (1) pertain to the maintenance of records 
that, in reasonable detail, accurately and fairly reflect the 
transactions and dispositions of the assets of the company; 
(2) provide reasonable assurance that transactions are 
recorded as necessary to permit preparation of financial 
statements in accordance with generally accepted 
accounting principles, and that receipts and expenditures 
of the company are being made only in accordance 
with authorisations of management and directors of the 
company; and (3) provide reasonable assurance regarding 
prevention or timely detection of unauthorised acquisition, 
use, or disposition of the company’s assets that could have 
a material effect on the financial statements.
Inherent Limitations of Internal Financial 
Controls With Reference to Consolidated 
Financial Statements
Because of the inherent limitations of internal financial 
controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements, including the possibility of collusion or improper 
management override of controls, material misstatements 
due to error or fraud may occur and not be detected. 
Also, projections of any evaluation of the internal financial 
controls with reference to consolidated financial statements 
to future periods are subject to the risk that the internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements may become inadequate because of changes in 
conditions, or that the degree of compliance with the policies 
or procedures may deteriorate.
Opinion
In our opinion, the Group, its associates, joint ventures 
and joint operation, which are companies incorporated in 
India, have, maintained in all material respects, adequate 
internal financial controls with reference to consolidated 
financial statements and such internal financial controls 
with reference to consolidated financial statements were 
operating effectively as at March 31, 2026, based on the 
internal control over financial reporting criteria established 
by the Holding Company considering the essential 
components of internal control stated in the Guidance Note 
issued by the ICAI.
Other Matters
Our report under Section 143(3)(i) of the Act on the 
adequacy and operating effectiveness of the internal 
financial controls with reference to consolidated financial 
statements of the Holding Company, in so far as it relates to 
15 subsidiaries, which are companies incorporated in India, 
is based on the corresponding reports of the auditors of 
such subsidiaries incorporated in India.

Group overview
	
Vedanta Limited (“the Company”) (CIN: 
L13209MH1965PLC291394) and its consolidated 
subsidiaries (collectively, the “Group”) is a diversified 
natural resource Group engaged in exploring, extracting 
and processing minerals and oil and gas. The Group 
engages in the exploration, production and sale of zinc, 
lead, silver, copper, aluminium, iron ore and oil and gas 
and has a presence across India, South Africa, Namibia, 
Ireland, Australia, Liberia and UAE. The Group is also in 
the business of commercial power generation, power 
cables, steel manufacturing and port operations in India 
and manufacturing of glass substrate in South Korea 
and Taiwan.
	
The Company was incorporated on 08 September 
1975 under the laws of the Republic of India. The 
registered office of the Company is situated at 1st Floor, 
‘C’ wing, Unit 103, Corporate Avenue, Atul Projects, 
Chakala, Andheri (East), Mumbai-400093, Maharashtra. 
The Company’s shares are listed on National Stock 
Exchange ('NSE') and Bombay Stock Exchange ('BSE') 
in India. In June 2007, the Company completed its initial 
public offering of American Depositary Shares, or ADS, 
each representing four equity shares, and listed its 
ADSs on the New York Stock Exchange ('NYSE').
	
The ADSs of the Company have been delisted from 
NYSE effective close of trading on NYSE on 08 
November 2021. The Company has been deregistered 
from SEC under the Exchange Act effective 01 
March 2023.
	
The Company is majority owned by Twin Star Holdings 
Limited (“Twin Star”), Vedanta Holdings Mauritius II 
Limited ("VHM2L"), Vedanta Holdings Mauritius Limited 
("VHML"), Welter Trading Limited (“Welter”) and Vedanta 
Netherlands Investments BV (“VNIBV”) which are in 
turn wholly-owned subsidiaries of Vedanta Resources 
Limited ("VRL"), a Company incorporated in the United 
Kingdom. VRL, through its subsidiaries, held 56.38% (31 
March 2025: 56.38%) of the Company's equity as at 31 
March 2026.
	
Details of Group’s various businesses are as follows. 
The Group’s percentage holdings in each of the below 
businesses are disclosed in note 44.
	
Continuing operations:
	•
Zinc India business is owned and operated by 
Hindustan Zinc Limited (“HZL”).
	•
 Zinc international business comprises Skorpion 
mine and refinery in Namibia operated through 
THL Zinc Namibia Holdings (Proprietary) Limited 
(“Skorpion”), Lisheen mine in Ireland operated 
through Vedanta Lisheen Holdings Limited 
(“Lisheen”) (Lisheen mine ceased operations in 
December 2015) and Black Mountain Mining 
(Proprietary) Limited (“BMM”), whose assets include 
the operational Black Mountain mine and the 
Gamsberg mine project located in South Africa.
	•
 The Group’s copper business owned and operated 
by the Company, Fujairah Gold FZC and Thalanga 
Copper Mines ("TCM") is principally one of custom 
smelting and includes captive power plants at 
Tuticorin in Southern India. A more detailed update 
on facilities at Tuticorin is given in note 3(c)(A)(iii).
	
Further, the Group’s copper business includes refinery 
and rod plant in Silvassa consisting of blister/ 
secondary material processing plant, a 2,22,000 TPA 
copper tank house plant and a copper rod mill with an 
installed capacity of 2,58,000 TPA. The plant continues 
to operate as usual, catering to the domestic market 
and export market.
	
In addition, the Group owns and operates a precious 
metal refinery and copper rod plant in Fujairah, UAE 
through its subsidiary Fujairah Gold FZC.
	•
 The Group's power business includes the wind 
power plants commissioned by HZL and a power 
plant at MALCO Energy Limited (“MEL”) (under care 
and maintenance) situated at Mettur Dam in the 
State of Tamil Nadu in southern India.
	•
 The Group’s other business also include Vizag 
General Cargo Berth Private Limited (“VGCB”). 
Vizag port project includes mechanization of coal 
handling facilities and upgradation of general 
cargo berth for handling coal at the outer harbour 
of Visakhapatnam Port on the east coast of 
India. VGCB commenced operations in the fourth 
quarter of fiscal 2013. The Group’s other business 
also includes AvanStrate Inc. (“ASI”), Vedanta 
Semiconductors Private Limited ("VSPL”), Vedanta 
Displays Limited (“VDL”), Ferro Alloys Corporation 
Limited ("FACOR") and Incab Industries limited 
("Incab"). ASI is involved in the manufacturing of 
glass substrate in South Korea and Taiwan. The 
Company acquired Vedanta Semiconductors Private 
Limited and Vedanta Displays Limited during FY 24 
for manufacturing semiconductor and display 
glass panels, respectively. FACOR is involved in 
manufacturing of Ferro Alloys, mining of chrome 
ore and generation of power. It owns a ferro chrome 
plant with a capacity of approximately 1,45,000 TPA, 
a 100 MW power plant and mines in Sukinda valley 
with current capacity of 1 MTPA. Incab is involved in 
in the business of power cables.
	
Discontinued operations:
	•
The Group’s oil and gas business is owned and 
operated by the Company and its subsidiary, Cairn 
Energy Hydrocarbons Limited ("CEHL") and consists 
of exploration, development and production of oil 
and gas.
	•
The Group’s Aluminium business is owned and 
operated by the Company and by Bharat Aluminium 
Company Limited (“BALCO”). The aluminium 
operations include a refinery and captive power plant 
at Lanjigarh, smelter and captive power plants at 
Jharsuguda and coal mines at Jamkhani, all situated 
in the State of Odisha in Eastern India. BALCO’s 
operations include two bauxite mines (operations 
currently being suspended), the Chotia coal block 
(operated and exhausted the coal reserves) and an 
unexplored coal block - Barra, a 1410 MW captive 
power plant (270 MW under suspension), 600MW 
independent power plant, an alumina refinery 
(operations of which have been suspended since 
September 2009), smelting and fabrication facilities 
in the State of Chhattisgarh in central India.
	•
The Group’s iron ore business is owned by the 
Company, and by its wholly owned subsidiaries, 
i.e., Sesa Resources Limited and Sesa Mining 
Corporation Limited and consists of exploration, 
mining, processing and trading of iron ore, pig iron 
and metallurgical coke and generation of power for 
captive use. Pursuant to the Hon'ble Supreme Court 
of India order, mining operations in the state of Goa 
were suspended. During the year ended 31 March 
2024, the Company had received environment 
clearance from the Ministry of Environment, Forest 
and Climate Change ("MoEFCC") and Consent 
to Operate ("CTO") from Goa State Pollution 
Board followed by commencement of Bicholim 
mining operations in March 2024 and the same is 
operational during the year.
	
During the previous year ended 31 March 2025, the 
Company received environment clearance from the 
MoEFCC for Cudnem mines Block VII and the other 
approvals are under process.
	
In addition, the Group’s iron ore business also includes 
a wholly owned subsidiary, Western Cluster Limited 
(“WCL”) in Liberia which has iron ore assets. WCL’s 
assets include development rights to Western Cluster 
and a network of iron ore deposits in West Africa. 
The mine operated from June 2022 to September 
2024, producing and selling DSO and generating low 
grade magnetite ore. Operations were suspended 
because the project became cash negative due to 
high stripping requirements, lower grade ore, and 
logistics constraints. Since the magnetite ore requires 
beneficiation, the Company plans to build concentrator 
plants in phases and is currently developing its own 
facility. Due to continued uncertainty in the viability of

(A)	 Basis of Consolidation
i)	
Subsidiaries:
	
The consolidated financial statements incorporate 
the financials statements of the Company and all 
its subsidiaries (the "Group"), being the entities that 
it controls.
	
Control is achieved where the Company:
	•
has power over the investee
	•
is exposed to, or has rights, to variable returns from 
its involvement with the investee; and
	•
has the ability to use its power to affect its returns
	
The Company reassess whether or not it controls an 
investee if facts and circumstances indicate that there 
are changes to one or more of the three elements of 
control listed above.
	
When the Company has less than majority of the 
voting rights of an investee, it has power over the 
investee when the voting rights are sufficient to give 
it the practical ability to direct the relevant activities of 
the investee unilaterally. The Company considers all 
relevant facts and circumstances in assessing whether 
or not the Company’s voting rights in an investee are 
sufficient to give it power, including;
	•
the size of the Company’s holding of voting rights 
relative to the size and dispersion of holdings of the 
other vote holders;
	•
potential voting rights held by the Company, other 
vote holders or other parties;
	•
rights arising from other contractual 
arrangements; and
	•
any additional facts and circumstances that indicate 
that the Company has, or does not have, the current 
ability to direct the relevant activities at the time that 
decisions need to be made, including voting patterns 
at previous shareholders’ meetings.
	
Consolidation of a subsidiary begins when the 
Company obtains control over the subsidiary and 
ceases when the Company loses control of the 
subsidiary. Specifically, income and expenses of a 
subsidiary acquired or disposed of during the year are 
included in the consolidated statement of profit and 
loss and other comprehensive income from the date 
the Company gains control until the date when the 
Company ceases to control the subsidiary.
	
The financial statements of subsidiaries are prepared 
for the same reporting year as the parent Company. 
Where necessary, adjustments are made to the 
financial statements of subsidiaries to align the 
accounting policies in line with accounting policies of 
the Group.
	
For non-wholly owned subsidiaries, a share of the 
profit/(loss) for the financial year and net assets is 
attributed to the non-controlling interests as shown 
in the consolidated statement of profit and loss and 
consolidated balance sheet.
	
Liability for put option issued to non-controlling 
interests which do not grant present access to 
ownership interest to the Group is recognised at 
present value of the redemption amount and is 
reclassified from equity. At the end of each reporting 
period, the non-controlling interests subject to put 
option is derecognised and the difference between 
the amount derecognised and present value of the 
redemption amount, which is recorded as a financial 
liability, is accounted for as an equity transaction.
	
For acquisitions of additional interests in subsidiaries, 
where there is no change in control, the Group 
recognises a reduction to the non-controlling interest of 
the respective subsidiary with the difference between 
this figure and the cash paid, inclusive of transaction 
fees, being recognised in equity. The results of 
subsidiaries acquired or disposed off during the year 
are included in the consolidated statement of profit and 
loss from the effective date of acquisition or up to the 
effective date of disposal, as appropriate.
	
Intra-Group balances and transactions, and any 
unrealized profit arising from intra-Group transactions, 
are eliminated. Unrealized losses are eliminated unless 
costs cannot be recovered.
ii)	
Joint arrangements
	
A Joint arrangement is an arrangement of which 
two or more parties have joint control. Joint control 
is considered when there is contractually agreed 
sharing of control of an arrangement, which exists 
only when decisions about the relevant activities 
require the unanimous consent of the parties sharing 
control. Investments in joint arrangements are 
classified as either joint operations or joint venture. 
The classification depends on the contractual rights 
and obligations of each investor, rather than the legal 
structure of the joint arrangement. A joint operation 
is a joint arrangement whereby the parties that have 
joint control of the arrangement have rights to the 
assets, and obligations for the liabilities, relating to the 
arrangement. A joint venture is a joint arrangement 
whereby, the parties that have joint control of 
the arrangement have rights to the net assets of 
the arrangement.
	
The Group has both joint operations and joint ventures.
	
Joint operations
	
The Group has joint operations within its Oil and gas 
segment. It participates in several unincorporated joint 
operations which involve the joint control of assets 
used in oil and gas exploration and producing activities. 
The Group accounts for its share of assets, liabilities, 
income and expenditure of joint operations in which the 
Group holds an interest. Liabilities in unincorporated 
joint operations, where the Group is the operator, 
is accounted for at gross values (including share 
of other partners) with a corresponding receivable 
from the venture partner. These have been included 
in the consolidated financial statements under the 
appropriate headings.
	
Details of joint operations are set out in Note 44.
	
Joint venture
	
The Group accounts for its interest in joint venture 
using the equity method (see (iv) below), after initially 
being recognised at cost in the consolidated balance 
sheet. Goodwill arising on the acquisition of joint 
venture is included in the carrying value of investments 
in joint venture.
iii)	
Investments in associates
	
Investments in associates are accounted for using the 
equity method (see (iv) below).
iv)	
Equity method of accounting
	
Under the equity method of accounting applicable 
for investments in associates and joint ventures, 
investments are initially recorded at the cost to the 
Group and then, in subsequent periods, the carrying 
value is adjusted to reflect the Group's share of the 
post-acquisition profits or losses of the investee, and 
the Group's share of other comprehensive income of 
the investee, other changes to the investee's net assets 
and is further adjusted for impairment losses, if any. 
Dividend received or receivable from associates and 
joint-ventures are recognised as a reduction in carrying 
amount of the investment.
	
The consolidated statement of profit and loss include 
the Group's share of investee's results, except where 
the investee is generating losses, share of such losses 
in excess of the Group's interest in that investee 
are not recognised. Losses recognised under the 
equity method in excess of the Group's investment in 
ordinary shares are applied to the other components 
of the Group's interest that forms part of Group's net 
investment in the investee in the reverse order of their 
seniority (i.e., priority in liquidation).

(v)	 Assets held for distribution and discontinued 
operations
	
The Group classifies assets and disposal groups as 
held for distribution if their carrying amounts will be 
recovered principally through a distribution rather 
than through continuing use. Actions required to 
complete the distribution should indicate that it is 
unlikely that significant changes to the distribution 
will be made or that the decision to distribution will be 
withdrawn. Management must be committed to the 
distribution expected within one year from the date 
of classification.
	
The criteria for held for distribution classification is 
regarded met only when the assets or disposal group 
is available for immediate distribution in its present 
condition, subject only to terms that are usual and 
customary for distribution of such assets (or disposal 
groups), its distribution is highly probable; and it will 
genuinely be distributed, not abandoned. The Group 
treats distribution of the asset or disposal group to be 
highly probable when:
	•
The appropriate level of management is committed 
to a plan to distribute the asset (or disposal group),
	•
The distribution is expected to qualify for recognition 
as a completed distribution within one year from the 
date of classification, and
	•
Actions required to complete the plan indicate that it 
is unlikely that significant changes to the plan will be 
made or that the plan will be withdrawn.
	
Non-current assets held for distribution to owners 
and disposal groups are measured at the lower of 
their carrying amount and the fair value less costs 
to distribute. Assets and liabilities classified as 
held distribution are presented separately in the 
balance sheet.
	
A disposal group qualifies as discontinued operation 
if it is a component of an entity that either has been 
disposed of, or is classified as held for sale, and:
	•
Represents a separate major line of business or 
geographical area of operations,
	•
Is part of a single co-ordinated plan to dispose of a 
separate major line of business or geographical area 
of operations.
	
Discontinued operations are excluded from the 
consolidated statement of profit and loss of continuing 
operations and are presented as a single amount as 
profit or loss before tax from discontinued operations 
in the consolidated statement of profit and loss. All 
notes to the consolidated financial statements mainly 
include amounts for continuing operations, unless 
otherwise mentioned. Notes relating to the assets and 
liabilities may not be strictly comparable as current year 
amounts would only pertain to continuing operations, 
unless otherwise stated.
	
Income and expenses and assets and liabilities are 
disclosed after netting off of transactions between 
continuing operations and discontinued operations 
in consolidated statement of profit and loss and 
consolidated balance sheet pursuant to compliance of 
Ind AS 110.
(B)	 Business combination
	
Business combinations are accounted for under the 
acquisition method. The acquiree's identifiable assets, 
liabilities and contingent liabilities that meet the 
conditions for recognition under Ind AS 103 ‘Business 
Combinations’ are recognised at their fair value at the 
acquisition date.
	
Excess of fair value of purchase consideration and 
the acquisition date non-controlling interest over 
the acquisition date fair value of identifiable assets 
acquired and liabilities assumed is recognised as 
goodwill. Goodwill arising on acquisitions is reviewed 
for impairment annually. Where the fair values of the 
identifiable assets and liabilities exceed the purchase 
consideration, the Group re-assesses whether it has 
correctly identified all of the assets acquired and all 
of the liabilities assumed and reviews the procedures 
used to measure the amounts to be recognised at the 
acquisition date. If the reassessment still results in an 
excess of the fair value of net assets acquired over 
the aggregate consideration transferred, then the gain 
is recognised in other comprehensive income and 
accumulated in equity as capital reserve. However, 
if there is no clear evidence of bargain purchase, the 
Group recognises the gain directly in equity as capital 
reserve, without routing the same through other 
comprehensive income.
	
Where it is not possible to complete the determination 
of fair values by the date on which the first post-
acquisition financial statements are approved, a 
provisional assessment of fair value is made and any 
adjustments required to those provisional fair values 
are finalised within 12 months of the acquisition date.
	
Those provisional amounts are adjusted through 
goodwill during the measurement period, or additional 
assets or liabilities are recognised, to reflect new 
information obtained about facts and circumstances 
that existed at the acquisition date that, if known, 
would have affected the amounts recognised at that 
date. These adjustments are called as measurement 
period adjustments. The measurement period does not 
exceed twelve months from the acquisition date.
	
Any non-controlling interest in an acquiree is measured 
at fair value or at the non-controlling interest's 
proportionate share of the acquiree's net identifiable 
assets. This accounting choice is made on a 
transaction by transaction basis.
	
Acquisition expenses are charged to the consolidated 
statement of profit and loss in the periods in which the 
costs are incurred and the services are received except 
costs to issue debt or equity securities which shall 
be recognised in accordance with Ind AS 32 and Ind 
AS 109.
	
If the Group acquires a Group of assets in a Company 
that does not constitute a business combination in 
accordance with Ind AS 103 ‘Business Combinations’, 
the cost of the acquired Group of assets is allocated 
to the individual identifiable assets acquired based on 
their relative fair value.
	
Common control transactions
	
A business combination involving entities or businesses 
under common control is a business combination in 
which all of the combining entities or businesses are 
ultimately controlled by the same party or parties both 
before and after the business combination and the 
control is not transitory. The transactions between 
entities under common control are specifically covered 
by Ind AS 103. Such transactions are accounted for 
using the pooling-of-interest method in accordance 
with Appendix C of IND AS 103. The assets and 
liabilities of the acquired entity are recognised at their 
carrying amounts recorded in the standalone financial 
statements of the acquired entity, except for certain 
income tax and deferred tax assets. No adjustments 
are made to reflect fair values or recognise any new 
assets or liabilities. The only adjustments that are 
made are to harmonise accounting policies.
	
The components of equity of the acquired companies 
are added to the same components within Group 
equity. The difference, if any, between the amounts 
recorded as share capital issued plus any additional 
consideration in the form of cash or other assets 
and the amount of share capital of the transferor 
is transferred to capital reserve and is presented 
separately from other capital reserves. The Company's 
shares issued in consideration for the acquired 
companies are recognised at face value from the 
moment the acquired companies are included in these 
financial statements and the financial statements of 
the commonly controlled entities would be combined, 
retrospectively, as if the transaction had occurred at 
the beginning of the earliest reporting period presented. 
However, the prior year comparative information is only 
adjusted for periods during which entities were under 
common control.

Interest income
	
Interest income from a financial asset is recognised
